#10457. Want to drive AI innovation? Talk about feelings

The 2026 midterms made one thing clear: Voters are “mad at” AI, as political strategist Rob Flaherty put it.

On the podcast Machine Gods, Flaherty notes that “the story people are saying to themselves is, ‘This thing is in my backyard. It is being used to train stuff that’s gonna take my job away, and I get no say over any of this, and I’m really mad about that.’” An NBC exit poll found that 56% of voters said that AI and data centers were a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress.

It’s obvious that people hate data centers. But workers resent AI rollouts in their workplaces, too. Data tracked on Blood in the Machine shows office worker sentiment toward AI dropped from 81% positive in 2019 to just 43% positive (with 53% negative) by 2026, listing “force-fed tools” as a major grievance. A Gallup global study reported that 74% of Americans are worried about AI, driven by widespread anxiety over job obsolescence and automated layoffs.

These voters are American employees, many of whom are being asked by their employers to “transform” their work lives with AI. You might be thinking: How can someone who voted against fast-moving AI on Tuesday be open and willing to experiment with AI at scale in their work lives? The answer is they can’t. We have a negative bias towards uncertainty, and our AI future is the ultimate uncertainty. Nobody knows what’s going to happen. And as we saw in the election, voters said, “Slow down.”

American employers need to deal with this fact. That doesn’t mean voters—or employees—hate AI. For most of us, AI offers a fundamental paradox: There’s a lot we like about generative AI, how it helps our daily lives. And we are fearful of it. We have to hold that duality.

This matters deeply to any manager or leader who wants their company to adopt AI at scale. When people are fearful and conflicted, they want to find safety. This means we resist change, or we act out against it. “An April 2026 survey of 2,400 knowledge workers across the U.S., U.K., and Europe—including 1,200 C-suite executives—conducted by Writer and Workplace Intelligence found that 29% of employees admitted to actively sabotaging their company’s AI strategy, a figure that jumps to 44% among Gen Z workers,” writes Fortune. It’s very hard to be open, innovative, and experimental when you fear for your future.

Nothing about the election results says stop AI entirely. It says, “Pause and let’s please talk about this.” This has to happen at work, too. In this article, I share how to get started, with two key questions.

Why can’t people change?

I spent decades as a political and advocacy consultant, and clients always asked me the same thing: Why won’t people change their behavior? Why don’t they vote for the candidates who support their interests? Why don’t they exercise? Why won’t they support a policy that will save them money and improve their health? Here’s what I learned, and science backs me up: You can’t change behavior when people are stuck. So why do people get stuck?

  • Change feels dangerous, and it’s safer to stay where you are.
  • We’ve built an “immunity to change.”

In Robert Kegan and Lisa Lahey’s Immunity to Change framework, the idea is that when we can’t make a change we genuinely want, it’s usually not a willpower problem. It’s because some part of us is committed—quietly, even unconsciously—to the opposite. Kegan calls this a psychological immune system. It has one foot on the gas and one on the brake.

When change feels unsafe, our brain, nervous system and body will conspire to keep us in the status quo. After all, its job is to keep us safe. Often, our psychological immune system is run by anxiety. Anxiety is a response to threats we anticipate.

Change with AI came too fast, too soon, too much, which creates a threat response in humans. We freeze, fight, or flee. In his new book, Our Existential Advantage, Enrique Rubio argues that every major technological revolution teaches the same lesson: Things change. Historically, though, the change came slowly enough for society to adjust. The printing press spread knowledge across Europe and helped spark the Renaissance and the Enlightenment, but that took decades. AI is just as transformative, and it’s happening almost overnight. Because the change is so fast, the structures built on the old technology can’t keep up, and nor can we. As a result, many people despair that AI is something that’s happening to us, that it’s inevitable and we don’t have any agency over it.

We feel anxious about AI for very good reason. It threatens our safety, our livelihoods, our children’s futures, our values, and the meaning that we find in work. I’ve heard from employees who resent AI for siphoning off creativity and expertise, or think that it encourages sloppiness or laziness. We work for many different reasons. Although money is important, humans highly value agency at work, and we need meaning and purpose. When we give decisions to AI, what happens to core values like self-reliance, learning, or usefulness? The scholar Ziyaad Bhorat proffers three important abilities that individuals and communities have already identified as worth protecting from AI: work, knowledge and understanding, and decision-making. He writes that work is worth protecting, as is the right to keep our skills from atrophying and from being substituted by machines.

On Election Day, voters took back agency over AI. Their employers need to listen, and it starts with having a different kind of conversation about AI and work.

How to have the right AI conversations

Recently I was a guest on Changing Conversations, a podcast hosted by Katherine Cotter and Stig Albertsen, who lead organizational transformation work at the consultancy Implement. We discussed the opportunity leaders have right now to start conversations with their teams that understand the fundamental paradox of AI, and offer space and time to explore it. These conversations don’t need to have clear next steps and a defined outcome; they simply need to happen.

We are having technical conversations about AI: the opportunity, where to focus, how to roll out transformation and increase proficiency. There’s a real sense of FOMO with AI, a real sense of you’ve got to get with the program. A lot of people feel like admitting any sense of hesitancy or fear might make them weak. They worry that asking questions about AI rollouts might cause them to be viewed as un-innovative, which is ironic, because when you’re feeling stuck, you’re not as innovative. So the key is to get unstuck, and that means digging into our emotions around what AI means to us.

AI brings up a lot of emotions, and most of us are uncomfortable with emotions at work. That’s why this stuff is so important: When you don’t feel your emotions, you can’t make the best decisions. I want people to make good decisions. So I want them to sit for a minute and have this conversation, because when we’re able to name difficult emotions, understand them, and move through, we are able to create change, innovation, and great new things. The threat diminishes and we see a way forward. We regain our agency.

And it can start by asking two simple questions: “When I think of my craft, what makes me feel proud, fulfilled, purposeful?” and then “Does the implementation of AI change anything about this?”

I like to ask people to think of the parts of their craft and work that they really love to do, and that they feel mastery over. For most people, this is a good feeling. When we think about our craft, we feel proud, and we feel a tremendous sense of agency because we have worked hard to master something valuable. And when we then unpack how AI relates to our craft, it can bring up a lot of questions. It can remind us where AI is aligned with our values, and where it’s not. It can make us think about whether AI threatens our craft, or can enhance it, or both. This conversation opens up room to explore more deeply the question of what our AI future means for us.

I think AI gives us an opportunity to face what many of us see as an existential threat and to move through that. That’s how we gain control. Stig noted, “AI…holds an invitation to figure out what is the uniqueness of being human, or even what is my unique gift…. Part of what I do can be handled by other means and supporting tools and technology, and that’s an invitation for me to figure out: What is it that cannot be distributed to someone else, because only I can do that with that specific flavor?”

Questions to ask yourself and your team

I asked Stig: After all the years you’ve been doing this work, what’s the piece of your craft you love most, the thing you’re really good at? Try that yourself, and see what comes up. Sit with it; don’t rush to solve it!

Here are some more helpful questions to ask yourself and your team:

  • What do I love about AI? What has surprised me?
  • What parts of my job do I dislike and wish AI would take?
  • What parts do I love and never want AI to touch? Why do they matter so much?
  • What scares me about AI?
  • What values are underneath all of that?

A few things I’ve learned from running these conversations: The leader goes first, and admits their own messiness. Expect the first few minutes to feel weird; people often look at me blankly until we get to their values or their kids, and then it clicks. Don’t attach a productivity goal. And make room for both/and, as the scholar Wendy Smith would put it. The most common thing I hear is some version of: I love it, it helps me so much, and I’m really worried about my kids.

People are relieved to learn they’re not the only ones holding both. The conversation is the most important part. There are no right or wrong answers, only the beginning of getting unstuck and moving through change.

#10456. How Motion Design Improves SaaS Onboarding and Feature Adoption

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most SaaS products don't lose users because the software is bad. They lose users in the first few minutes, before anyone has seen what the product can actually do. Someone signs up, lands on an empty dashboard, feels a flicker of confusion, and quietly leaves. The industry has a name for the gap between signing up and getting value: activation. Closing it is one of the hardest problems in product design.

Motion design is one of the most underused tools for closing that gap. Used well, animation isn't decoration sprinkled on at the end. It's a layer of communication that tells users where to look, confirms that their actions worked, and makes a complex interface feel learnable instead of overwhelming. This article looks at why motion influences behaviour during onboarding, the specific patterns that move the needle on activation and feature adoption, and how to build them responsibly as a developer — with an eye on performance and accessibility throughout.

Motion works in onboarding because it speaks to how human perception actually operates, not because it looks modern. A few principles do most of the heavy lifting.

It directs attention. The eye is drawn to movement before it reads a single word. A gently pulsing button or an element that slides into view tells a new user where to go next without a paragraph of instructions. On a crowded first-run screen, that guidance is the difference between a confident first action and a confused exit.

It preserves context. When a panel expands, a card flips, or a new view slides in from the right, a short transition shows users where things came from and where they went. This spatial continuity keeps people oriented. Interfaces that snap instantly between states force the user to re-scan the screen each time and silently rebuild their mental model.

It confirms actions. Every click, toggle, and form submission is a small question: did that work? A quick visual response — a checkmark drawing itself, a row settling into place — answers it immediately. Without that feedback, users repeat actions, doubt the system, or assume something broke.

It shapes perceived performance. A thoughtful loading animation or skeleton screen makes a wait feel shorter and the product feel responsive, even when the underlying request takes exactly as long. Perception of speed is part of the experience, and motion is how you manage it.

These are the patterns that reliably help new users reach their first win.

Onboarding doesn't end after the first session. Most SaaS products keep shipping features, and each one faces its own adoption problem: users settle into a few familiar workflows and never discover the rest. Motion is how you reintroduce the product to people who already think they know it.

Contextual nudges that appear in motion — a tooltip that eases in near a newly relevant button, a gentle highlight on a feature the moment a user hits the limit it solves — are far more effective than a generic email. They arrive at the point of need and use movement to pull attention without hijacking the screen.

"What's new" reveals can announce an update with a small, well-timed animation rather than a modal that gets dismissed on reflex. A badge that animates in, or a panel that slides open on the first visit to a page, respects the user's flow while still being noticed.

Animated demonstrations carry the most weight for genuinely complex features. Showing a feature in motion — rather than describing it in text — lets users grasp a multi-step workflow in seconds. For intricate capabilities, this is where a short, purpose-made explainer earns its place, a point we return to in the next section.

The right tool depends on how complex the animation is and where it lives. Roughly in order of weight:

CSS transitions and keyframe animations should be your default. They cover the large majority of onboarding motion — hovers, state changes, highlights, progress bars — and the browser can run them efficiently. Reach for JavaScript only when CSS genuinely can't express what you need.

The Web Animations API gives you CSS-level performance with programmatic control, which matters when animations depend on data or user input, or need to be sequenced and interrupted. SitePoint's guide to the Web Animations API is a solid introduction, and the broader web animation archive covers libraries like GSAP for orchestrating complex timelines.

Lottie is the bridge between designer-made animation and the web. Designers export vector animations as JSON, and a lightweight player renders them natively at small file sizes — ideal for polished illustrative moments like success states and animated empty states, without hand-coding every frame.

Pre-rendered video is the right call when a feature is genuinely involved and a looping CSS animation or a tooltip simply can't carry the explanation. A short, well-produced walkthrough can compress a multi-step workflow into something a user absorbs in under a minute, which is why many teams lean on a dedicated SaaS explainer video for their most complex features and onboarding moments. The trade-off is weight and production effort, so reserve video for the handful of places where it genuinely outperforms in-interface motion, lazy-load it, and never autoplay it with sound.

Motion that stutters does more damage than no motion at all, and motion that ignores accessibility can actively harm users. Two disciplines keep animation on the right side of that line.

For performance, animate the properties the browser can handle cheaply: transform and opacity. These can run on the compositor thread without triggering layout or paint, which is what lets animation hold a smooth 60fps. Animating properties like width, height, top, or left forces the browser to recalculate layout on every frame and is the usual cause of janky motion. Keep animations short — most interface transitions should land between 150 and 300 milliseconds — because motion that overstays its welcome makes a product feel slow.

For accessibility, honour the prefers-reduced-motion media query. Some users experience dizziness, nausea, or disorientation from movement, and the operating system lets them ask for less of it. Respecting that setting is straightforward:

Beyond that, never let an animation block interaction. If a user has to wait for a flourish to finish before they can click, the motion is working against them. Animation should support the task and then get out of the way.

Motion design is a product decision, so treat it like one and measure it. The metrics that matter map directly to the problems motion is meant to solve.

Treat animations as hypotheses and A/B test them. Ship the animated onboarding step to half of your new users and measure activation against the control. Motion should earn its place with data, not assumptions — and occasionally the data will tell you an animation is slowing people down, which is just as useful to know.

The best onboarding motion is the kind users never consciously notice. It simply makes the product feel clear, responsive, and easy to learn — guiding attention, confirming actions, and turning a complex interface into something approachable. That's the real payoff: not animation for its own sake, but fewer confused users, faster time to value, and features that actually get discovered.

Start small. Pick the single point in your onboarding where users most often stall, add one purposeful animation that removes the confusion, and measure what happens. Motion, used deliberately, is one of the most direct levers you have on activation and adoption — and like any good tool, it works best when it draws no attention to itself.

The Garmin Fenix E and Garmin Venu 3S are for two different types of people, but both are available at a surprisingly low price thanks to these limited-time Garmin deals.

Garmin watches are often expensive, which is why I always recommend them on sale. For example, the Garmin Fenix E, usually $799, is now down to $399. That’s the all-time low price for this model and probably the best Garmin deal I’ve seen so far this fall.

The Garmin Fenix E is essentially a Garmin Epix Gen 2 with a newer OS. It sports multi-GNSS navigation plus a 3-axis compass, gyroscope, and barometric altimeter that should cover basically all your tracking needs. It’s got pulse ox monitoring, respiration tracking, advanced sleep monitoring, real-time stamina tracking, and a training readiness score (so you know what days you should be taking it easy).

Despite all the features, this one will last you two weeks per charge and can utilize GPS for up to 42 hours on each charge. The stainless steel bezel looks great, and the 47mm fiber-reinforced polymer case is built to last. This is one of those watches that, quite frankly, makes no sense at full cost. At half the price, though? Yeah, that looks much better.

If you’re looking for something a little more elegant-looking, the Garmin Venu 3S is the right choice. At $299, this Garmin deal makes it $250 less than the Garmin Venu 4. You might think buying the newest one is automatically better, but that’s not necessarily the case between these two models.

For example, the Venu 4 is thicker and heavier because it uses an all-metal casing, has one less button on the side, lacks the permanent hour markers that are on the Venu 3S’s bezel, and has worse battery life by 1-2 days, depending on your usage. The Venu 4 has more features and a newer OS, but I personally like the OS design on the 3S better (and I’m apparently not alone on that front).

The Venu 4 also has new sleep guidance and coaching features, training load and several tools that used to be for Garmin Forerunner watches, plus lifestyle logging, but I’m not sure I’d want to pay $250 to get those. Either way, you’ve got a great option now that the Venu 3S is at such a fantastic price.

#10453. What I let AI touch in my solo business—and what stays off-limits

A lot of AI advice suggests that you hand over work to a personal agent, like letting it triage your inbox or shop for you. That’s certainly appealing, since we’re all relentlessly busy and constantly fighting small tasks that take up our time. 

But every time you connect an AI tool to one of your accounts, you’re also answering a second question: What is this tool allowed to do on my behalf? 

For a lot of solopreneurs, that question gets answered by default. You click “allow” on the permissions screen, and the tool can now reach everything in that account. 

I use AI a lot in my business, but I’ve also drawn some very clear boundaries around what it can access.

Sort your tools by what AI can do in them

Every AI tool I use falls into one of three buckets.

Read but not edit. AI can pull information from the tool, but it can’t change anything. This works well for reference material you want AI to draw from without any risk of it being rewritten.

One example, for me, is pulling financial data from QuickBooks. I let Claude analyze some numbers every month, but I don’t want AI making changes to my transactions.

Full editing. AI can create and change things directly in these tools. This makes sense where a mistake is easy to spot and quick to undo.

I use Canva to plan a lot of my marketing material. Nothing is mission-critical, and the full ability to make changes gives me a lot of capabilities to use Claude with Canva.

Off-limits. AI can’t access the tool at all. 

One thing I don’t let AI touch at all is my bank accounts. JP Morgan Chase reported that people were handing over their banking credentials to AI agents like Muse. That’s outside of my comfort zone. 

Workarounds can ease your comfort with AI access 

Some of my most useful setups give AI partial access to a tool. 

Secondary accounts. You might give AI its own limited version of a tool and keep it out of your main account.

I do this with email. I have a secondary email inbox for inbound inquiries to my website. AI can sort and draft replies without touching my main inbox.

Limited permissions

Some tools will let you scope AI to certain projects. I use a database tool called Airtable to manage information for my solo business. Claude can only access certain parts of Airtable, so it can’t inadvertently cause an issue in a tool that I rely on heavily. 

“Supervised” tasks. AI does the work, and nothing moves forward until I approve it. With my email example, Claude can draft a reply to an email but can’t send it. The draft waits for me to review it.

Revisit the boundaries as the tools change

Your boundaries may change over time. AI tools keep adding new connections and capabilities. These changes may make you more or less comfortable with what they can do.

Or you might need to “use AI to fight AI.” I was resistant to letting AI access my email inbox, but the inbound inquiries I get from other people using AI themselves forced me to think differently. My solution was the separate email inbox. 

In the end, I can use AI as much as I do because I decided up front what it can access.

#10450. Tag yourself as one of USPS’s new cryptid stamps

At the annual Mothman Festival in Point Pleasant, West Virginia, tens of thousands of visitors gather in their finest cosplay to commemorate the 1966 day that the “Mothman”—a 7-foot moth creature with bright red eyes—supposedly appeared from either the depths of hell or outer reaches of space to terrify onlookers. The festival is full of Mothman fans, for whom the legendary cryptid has morphed from a haunting specter to more of a lovable hero. Now, he’s getting his own official stamp. 

On November 9, the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) released an initial batch of stamp subjects for 2027. They run the gamut from traditional, subject-centric designs, like a stamp commemorating baseball’s Willie Mays, to designs aimed at a more artistic crowd, like a series of whimsical watercolor unicorns. 

The “Mythical Creatures” collection is a lineup of five American cryptids—the Mothman, Jackalope, Sasquatch, Squonk, and Champ—each designed by Antonio Alcalá, an art director at USPS, and illustrated by Nat Power, a tattoo artist. They’re sure to please folk historians, stamp collectors, and Reddit users alike. 

Meet Squonk, Jackalope, and Champ

Every year, USPS’s Citizen’s Stamp Advisory Committee (CSAC) restarts an intensive process of sifting through thousands of suggested topics from the public to land on the 20-25 new designs it recommends be produced. According to a 2024 USPS blog post, the final list has to be “uniquely American” and balance nods to topics like science, arts, history, and culture. The process leads to selections that traverse an array of genres, from Toni Morrison to Spongebob Squarepants.

The Mythical Creatures collection merges art history with American folklore. Its subjects are spooky, unknowable creatures that emerged in different regions of the U.S. The Jackalope is part of Wyoming legend after two taxidermist brothers created an antlered bunny in the 1930s; the Squonk is a Pennsylvania-based, pig-like cryptid whose main attribute of note is its constant weeping; and the Champ is a lake monster hailing from the Lake Champlain region in New York and Vermont.

The designs from Alcalá and Power take these myths and interpret them through the lens of American traditional tattoo aesthetics, rendering them in bold, dark lines with bright washes of color. The final products look less like the fare of an older letter-writing crowd, and more like the art you might find on the arm of a millennial who’s fallen down a few too many Reddit rabbit holes. 

In the 2024 blog post, Joe Kelley, the CSAC chair and a stamp collector, explained that the multigenerational appeal is often the point: “We want to highlight what’s great about America. The hope is to not only draw more people to the hobby of stamp collecting, but also encourage people to simply use stamps. With so much emphasis today on the popularity of all things ‘retro,’ why not be retro yourself and write a letter?”

#10448. A design legend’s oddball watches are back and cooler than ever

Tibor Kalman, the graphic designer, was known for confrontational stances; a “self-styled bad boy” of his profession, as The New York Times once described him. But Kalman—who was the editor in chief of Colors magazine and created album covers for The Talking Heads—produced plenty that was witty and warm before he died a quarter of a century ago, at age 49. Notably, this included a series of charming and celebrated wristwatches that his son, Alex, brought back into production. 

Analog watches may not seem like the most buzzy category in 21st-century retail, but these have, “for lack of a better word, a bit of a timeless design quality,” Alex Kalman says. In fact, design aficionados may recognize the three watches that have gone on sale this week through the website of M&Co Labs, Tibor’s design-product studio. They were originally part of a larger watch series tracing back to the late 1980s and early 1990s in which the elder Kalman treated the watch face as a space to subtly comment on time itself.

The watches became a flagship product for M&Co. In different ways, each gently challenges the functionality of a watch. One of them, dubbed “10-4-1,” eliminates all the hour numbers except for those three; it’s in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art. Another, “Onomatopoeia,” replaces some numbers with tiny pictograms: a cat for 9, an egg for 12. The third, “Askew” simply jumbles the numbers, apparently at random. On the back, all three are inscribed “Waste Not A Moment.” 

Today, the watches’ slightly impractical interfaces are arguably more subversive than when they were introduced. “It’s very funny that there’s all this effort for frictionless design, here is something so elemental as a watch face, but one that creates friction in trying to read the time on it,” Alex says. The urge to eliminate friction was present in Tibor’s era, but today it sometimes seems to be design’s primary function. “It’s come so much further than what he was initially reacting to,” Alex adds. And maybe that means it’s a perfect time for the watches to return.

Kalman became known for a distinct point of view, pushing his profession to face its social responsibilities, and tackling issues like race and AIDS in Colors. He also had a slew of client work, including design for musicians and the Times Square Redevelopment Corporation, under the auspices of M&Co. (The “M” stood for his wife and collaborator Maira Kalman, the artist, writer, and children’s book author.) In addition to the watches, the M&Co Labs spinoff produced a variety of clever objects, such as a paperweight shaped like crumpled paper, that were popular with the design-savvy set. 

After Tibor died in 1999, Alex says, Maira focused on her own work, making licensing deals with other firms to manage M&Co Labs’ product line. While the watches stayed in distribution for years, that supplier relationship eventually fizzled, and they fell out of production.

More recently, Maira and Alex (who is also a filmmaker and founder/curator of Mmuseumm, a mini-museum in a former freight elevator in lower Manhattan), decided to produce new batches of a few of the watches. It’s a tentative first step toward bringing back M&Co as a family business of sorts. 

“All the products, as the family likes to do, look at the conventions of things and play with them a little bit,” Alex says.

And that speaks to the potential appeal of the oddball, winky watches right now. When they were brand new, the watches were a means of “thinking of incredibly common vernacular everyday items that are part of our lives,” Alex says, “and how to play with them with that particular sensibility and share those ideas through everyday products, rather than just through design or editorial work.”

In a way, a time-keeping object’s role as material signifier of modernity is even more acute now that we track time on digital devices. A glance checking the hour may also bring news of a new follower, or a catastrophe. All the more reason, perhaps, to pause over that routine moment of noting where the clock stands. 

“The faces themselves, which is obviously really where the character is, have a lot of soul and wit and humanism,” Alex says. “And I think that’s a really nice thing to offer people in our increasingly slick technological landscape.”

It doesn’t hurt that for some the watches are both iconic and nostalgic, classic symbols of a distinct moment in product-design history with a certain pre-smartphone status. At least, this new iteration of M&Co Labs will find out if it’s true that there’s something meaningful in bringing these objects back. If it goes well, they’ll try physical retail: “Either on the corner of Canal Street or the MoMA Store,” Alex jokes.

#10445. Why Your AI Agent Can't Read the Web (and How to Build a Fetch Layer That Can)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

This is the least glamorous part of building with LLMs and it's where a lot of agent projects quietly fall over. The model is rarely the problem. The fetch is. In this article we'll look at why live web retrieval has become so unreliable for AI tools, what the numbers say about the shift, and how to build a small, well-behaved fetch layer in Python that fails loudly instead of feeding your model garbage.

A few years ago, a plain requests.get() worked on most of the public web. That's no longer true, and the reason is simple: there are now more bots than people.

According to the 2025 Imperva Bad Bot Report, automated traffic made up 51% of all web traffic in 2024. That's the first time in a decade it has passed human activity. Bad bots alone (scrapers, credential stuffers, scalpers) went from 32% to 37% of traffic in a single year.

Source: Imperva Bad Bot Report 2024 and 2025

From a site owner's point of view, your polite research agent and a credential-stuffing botnet look much the same at the network edge. Both are non-browser clients making fast requests from data-center IP ranges. So the defaults have tightened. In July 2025 Cloudflare began blocking known AI crawlers by default for new customers, and bot management products now look at TLS fingerprints, header order, IP reputation and JavaScript execution, not just the User-Agent string.

It helps to understand the publisher's side of the deal, because it explains why your agent is being treated with suspicion.

Cloudflare splits AI crawling into three purposes: training (collecting data to train models), search (building an index for AI search answers) and user action (fetching a page because a person just asked a question). Training dominates.

Training crawls take content and send nothing back. Cloudflare measures this with a crawl-to-referral ratio: how many pages a platform crawls for every visitor it sends to the site. In its crawl-to-click gap analysis, the ratios for some AI platforms ran into the tens of thousands, compared with single digits for traditional search.

If you ran a publication and saw those numbers, you'd block too. The catch is that blocking is usually done by user agent or IP range, so it hits user-action fetches as well. Those are the ones that happen when a person asks your agent to read a specific article, and Cloudflare's 2025 Year in Review found they grew more than 15x during the year. Your agent is caught in a fight it didn't start.

The mix of crawlers also shifts quickly, which makes static allow and block lists fragile on both sides:

And restrictions keep piling up. The Consent in Crisis study audited 14,000 web domains and found that a large and fast-growing share of the sources behind the C4 training corpus now restrict AI crawlers, either through robots.txt or their terms of service.

Source: Longpre et al., Consent in Crisis (NeurIPS 2024)

So that's the environment your agent fetches in. Here's how to build for it.

Before writing any retry logic, put names on your failures. "The request failed" is useless to both you and the model. In practice almost every failed fetch falls into one of four buckets:

Bucket 2 is the dangerous one, because a block page often comes back with a 200 OK. If you don't check, the model will happily summarise "Checking your browser before accessing..." as if it were the article.

Here's a compact fetch layer in Python using httpx and the standard library's robots.txt parser. It's around 100 lines and covers the four buckets above.

Use a descriptive user agent with a contact URL. It costs you nothing and site operators are far more likely to allow a client they can identify and reach. Then check robots.txt (standardised as RFC 9309) before every new host.

The lru_cache means you fetch robots.txt once per origin rather than once per page. In a long-running service you'll want a cache with a TTL instead, since robots.txt files do change.

This is the core of the layer. Instead of returning raw HTML, return a result that says which bucket you landed in.

The marker list is deliberately simple. It won't catch every interstitial, but it catches the common ones, and a false "blocked" is much cheaper than a confident summary of a CAPTCHA page. Log every blocked result with its first few hundred characters so you can grow the list from real data.

Retries should depend on the bucket. Throttled and broken responses get exponential backoff with jitter. Blocked and not-allowed responses get no retries at all.

Note the cap on wait. A site sending Retry-After: 3600 is telling you to go away for an hour. An interactive agent should report that to the user rather than block a request thread for that long.

The cheapest fetch is the one you don't make. Agents often re-read the same documentation page several times in one session. Store the ETag and Last-Modified headers and send them back as If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. A 304 Not Modified response costs the server almost nothing and lowers the odds of being rate limited.

Wire these into fetch() by passing headers=conditional_headers(url) to client.get(). On a 304, return the cached text. On a 200, call remember().

Finally, don't hide failures from the LLM. Give the tool output a structured shape so the model can reason about it:

(extract_main_text is whatever readability or boilerplate-removal step you already use. Libraries like trafilatura work well here.)

With this in place, the model's answer changes from a made-up summary to "I couldn't read that page because the site blocks automated access. Here's what I found from two other sources." That's a better product, and it builds trust with users.

Once you've done everything above, some legitimate user-action fetches will still fail. That's usually because the site blocks data-center IP ranges outright, not because of anything your agent did. Teams handle this in a few ways, roughly in order of preference:

The principle is the same in every case: the network path is a reliability decision, not a way around a site's wishes. Your robots.txt check and your honest user agent should stay in place whichever route the request takes.

Once your fetch layer returns structured results, observability is easy. Emit one event per fetch with the host, status bucket and latency, and watch these:

If you're prototyping agents with AI coding assistants, ask them to generate these metrics hooks from the start. They're easy to bolt on now and painful to add later. For a sense of how well current tools handle this kind of infrastructure code, Vibe Coder Journal publishes hands-on reviews and benchmarks of AI coding tools.

The web your agent reads in 2026 isn't the open, fetch-anything web many of us learned on. More than half the traffic is automated, publishers have good reasons to be wary of AI crawlers, and the defaults now lean toward blocking. You can't change that. You can make your agent a good citizen, though: one that identifies itself, respects the rules, backs off when asked, and tells the truth when it can't read something.

Most of the reliability gains come from the unglamorous parts: classifying failures, caching and passing honest errors to the model. Get those right and your agent will feel much more dependable, even on the days when half the web won't let it in.

It depends on the jurisdiction, the site's terms of service and what you do with the content. Respecting robots.txt and site terms is the baseline. For commercial products, get proper legal advice.

Many site owners expect it to, and RFC 9309 makes no exception for user-triggered fetches. The safest default is to obey it and tell the user when a page is disallowed.

Many bot-protection systems serve a challenge page with a 200 status. Check the body for challenge markers before passing it to the model, as in the looks_blocked() function above.

Only for pages that render their main content with JavaScript. Try a plain HTTP fetch first. Headless browsers are slower, cost more to run and are easier to fingerprint.

#10444. Democrats won Congress. What might happen to Trump’s construction projects now?

The future of President Donald Trump’s construction and renovation projects in Washington, D.C., could soon come into question, after Democrats take control of Congress in January.

Trump has powered his pet projects through by sheer force of will since retaking office last year, setting a breakneck pace for ideas moving from blueprint to construction site. Disregarding legally mandated approval processes and protocols, his administration has knocked down buildings and torn up trees without permission.

Though legal challenges have, at times, slowed projects like the White House ballroom, arch monument, a D.C. golf course, and John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts renovations, they haven’t been effective.

The landscape is shifting, however. Once the the next Democrat-led Congress is in place, changes to the built environment will face oversight that Republicans didn’t previously provide. This is how it might shake out.

3 new roadblocks to Trump’s projects

First, Democrats will get two ex officio seats on the 12-person National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC)—the federal government’s D.C.-area planning agency—that are reserved for U.S. Senate and House of Representatives members. The president appoints some members of the commission, and there are others who are there because of their job titles.

Democrats will replace Senator Rand Paul and Representative James Comer, both Kentucky Republicans, with their own people. Those two new members of the commission could join with the District of Columbia’s four members, who have consistently voted against Trump’s building priorities, to block his projects from passing with a tied 6-6 vote.

Second, Democrats will have standing to sue in federal court on behalf of the Senate and House, using Senate and House counsel. Leveraging congressional subpoenas and investigations, lawmakers could learn more about private donations Trump used to fund the projects.

Third, and most important, Democrats will hold the purse strings in the appropriations process, which means they can restrict or defund executive branch activities. In addition to accepting private donations, Trump has also funded his construction with public, taxpayer funds. Under Democrats, that practice could soon come to an end.

What Democrats are saying

These potential roadblocks could be why Trump seems to be rushing to get construction work done before the next Congress is sworn in. The day after the midterm elections, Trump signed and raised a beam at the ballroom site. Meanwhile, the NCPC approved plans for his arch the following day, though a judge issued a temporary restraining order shortly after.

The restraining order lasts just 14 days, and Democratic lawmakers are gearing up to fight it long term.

Speaking about Trump’s arch, Representative Don Beyer, the Democrat whose northern Virginia district includes Arlington National Cemetery, said at a press conference Friday that he’s “never seen a project with such profound, widespread opposition from the very people who it will affect most.”

To fight the project, Beyer authored the Arlington National Cemetery Viewshed Protection Act, which would block the arch’s construction outright. Introduced in May, the bill hasn’t been brought to a vote under Republican House leadership. Under Democrats, that and similar legislation to defund or explicitly ban Trump projects could more easily make it to a vote.

Representative Jared Huffman, a California Democrat and ranking member on the House Natural Resources Committee, which oversees the Department of the Interior, said “the ground between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington belongs to the American people and the families who have buried loved ones there.” He warned officials who keep the project moving forward or firms that sign on to build the arch to “understand the legal risk they’re taking on.”

“If Trump wants a tribute to himself, he can build one at one of his glitzy resorts or private golf clubs,” Huffman said Friday in a statement. “Come January, a new Congress will demand answers from the people enabling this abuse of our public lands and our laws.”

For two years, Trump hasn’t faced pushback from Congress over his construction projects. That’s about to change.

#10441. Bending Spoons is buying up the internet. Can its business model last?

Bending Spoons has already acquired some of the internet’s most recognizable software brands. And it has identified more than 1,000 others it could potentially acquire.

The Milan-based company, whose portfolio includes Evernote, WeTransfer, Vimeo, AOL, and Eventbrite, disclosed the figure in its IPO prospectus. Together, those potential targets generated nearly $400 billion in estimated revenue in 2025.

Bending Spoons has hardly slowed down since its stock market debut in July. It has completed acquisitions of Airtable and Miro, and in October, Berkshire Hathaway invested another $330 million, bringing its ownership stake to 4%.

Its business model—buy an established product with paying customers, reorganize the company, reduce costs, improve the technology, and use the profits to pursue more acquisitions—is attracting attention across the software industry. And the results have generally been impressive.

But so have the job cuts. As AI makes software cheaper to develop and maintain, Bending Spoons may now be establishing a new model for an industry accustomed to prioritizing growth over profitability.

WHY BUYING OLD SOFTWARE MAKES FINANCIAL SENSE

Building a successful software business is expensive. A company could spend years developing a product, attracting customers, and trying to persuade them to pay for it with no guarantee it will succeed. Buying an established business, however, reduces some of that uncertainty.

“From an investor’s perspective, the fundamental advantage is that you’re buying proven behavior rather than financing the search for it,” says Vince Molinari, a financial services expert and founder and CEO of Fintech Media Group.

An established product already has customers, revenue, brand recognition, and a distribution network. For an acquirer, the opportunity often lies in improving how the business operates. Molinari places particular importance on customer retention. A company with loyal subscribers and inefficient operations may be more attractive than a fast-growing business whose customers regularly leave.

“Revenue tells you what customers paid yesterday. Retention helps tell you whether they’ll still be paying tomorrow,” he tells Fast Company.

Bending Spoons’ second-quarter results illustrate the appeal. Revenue rose 126% from a year earlier to $704 million, while operating income increased 139% to $240 million.

But acquisitions accounted for most of the revenue growth. Looking at its businesses without the extra revenue added by acquisitions, growth was just 3%. The figures show how heavily the company’s expansion still depends on buying businesses, rather than growing revenue from the ones it owns. “The next billion-dollar opportunity doesn’t necessarily start with the next big idea,” says Nadja Atwal, an international business adviser. “Sometimes it starts with recognizing that someone else’s old big idea still has plenty of life left in it.”

THE COST OF MAKING SOFTWARE MORE PROFITABLE

Bending Spoons is unusually willing to make sweeping changes after an acquisition. Its IPO filing disclosed that AOL, Eventbrite, and Vimeo collectively brought approximately 1,830 full-time-equivalent employees into the company. According to the filing, Bending Spoons planned to retain only a few hundred of those employees after restructuring the businesses.

The scale of such restructuring has attracted much criticism, but Vimeo offers an example of how Bending Spoons believes its approach can improve acquired products.

At Vimeo, Bending Spoons reported more than 30 product improvements during the second quarter, alongside a roughly 90% reduction in system-stability incidents compared with pre-acquisition levels. Uploads and searches also became at least 30% faster, according to the company.

These are encouraging results, although they are company-reported figures. Improvements in speed and reliability don’t necessarily tell us how customers feel about pricing, support, or the product’s direction.

Matteo Danieli, Bending Spoons’ cofounder and VP of product, told Fast Company⁠ last month that the company’s acquisition-driven growth gives its teams more freedom to concentrate on improving existing products. “We do not necessarily need to prove massive growth on products, and so we are actually free to focus on what’s useful for users,” he said.

Eliminating duplicated expenses, consolidating infrastructure, and improving how products are sold can make an acquired business substantially more profitable. But lower operating costs alone cannot establish whether a company is becoming healthier. Cutting too deeply can also mean losing experienced employees and the knowledge needed to maintain and improve a product.

“You can make almost any company look better for several quarters by cutting enough people and expenses. The real test is what happens three or five years later,” Molinari says.

Customers may judge the changes differently from investors. Faster software and new features can improve their experience, but higher prices, declining support, or unwanted product changes could weaken the loyalty that made these businesses attractive to acquire in the first place.

AI COULD CHANGE THE ECONOMICS EVEN FURTHER

Bending Spoons is betting that AI will help it accomplish more with smaller teams, and its own software-development figures suggest how quickly the technology is becoming part of its operations.

In its IPO prospectus, the company estimated that AI authored or coauthored more than 90% of software-code changes submitted for review by the end of March 2026, compared with less than 10% a year earlier.

That doesn’t mean AI independently builds or maintains its products. Engineers still have to review code, make decisions, and ensure software works reliably. But it demonstrates how extensively the company has incorporated AI into development.

Mohamed Mohamed, founder and CEO of applied AI company SmartBricks⁠ and a venture scout at a16z Speedrun, believes the implications could extend well beyond Bending Spoons’ engineering costs.

“AI is rapidly reducing the cost of developing, maintaining, and improving software,” he says. “That potentially makes acquiring established software businesses even more attractive because an acquirer can operate them with a fundamentally different cost structure.”

Marina Mogilko, an entrepreneur, investor, and creator who hosts the podcast Silicon Valley Girl, sees a parallel in the creator economy. She points to Electrify Video Partners’ majority investment in Veritasium, the popular science YouTube channel founded by Derek Muller. Electrify provides operational and commercial support while Muller retains an ownership interest and continues creating content.

“Centralizing operations, hiring, and monetization under one roof frees creative teams to focus on their craft, while giving the buyer decades of built-in brand trust and organic distribution that would cost a fortune to build from scratch today,” Mogilko says.

The comparison, while poignant, also has its limits. At Veritasium, for example, Muller remains central to the business, while Bending Spoons has often replaced much of the original workforce at companies it acquires. And that raises a question about how much institutional knowledge an acquirer can afford to lose while reorganizing a business.

CAN BENDING SPOONS KEEP ITS ADVANTAGE?

The reality is that the same AI tools that could make Bending Spoons’ acquisitions more profitable may also make the software it buys easier to compete against. As AI coding tools lower development costs, smaller teams can increasingly build products that once required far greater resources, putting pressure on established businesses to give customers compelling reasons to stay.

Cheaper software development could also change how investors value the businesses they acquire. “I believe we’re moving towards a world where the value of a software company is increasingly determined by the assets surrounding its technology rather than the technology itself,” SmartBricks⁠’ Mohamed says. That would give established software businesses an advantage only if their customers, distribution networks, and other assets remain difficult for competitors to replicate.

Bending Spoons has advantages that would be difficult for newcomers to match, including acquisition experience, access to financing, and an expanding technical operation. But acquisitions require capital, and the company ended June with approximately $4.09 billion in net debt. That increases the importance of generating lasting returns from the businesses it buys.

Mohamed believes those returns should be measured beyond immediate improvements in profitability. “Ultimately, the sustainability of this model depends on whether customer lifetime value improves, not simply whether EBITDA increases,” he says.

The list of more than 1,000 prospective acquisitions suggests that finding companies to buy is unlikely to be its immediate problem. But acquiring more businesses also means taking responsibility for the products and customer relationships that made them valuable. Mogilko thinks the biggest test comes after the deal closes.

“The real question—and the biggest risk to this model’s long-term sustainability—is how you maintain the soul of the company after replacing the original team and raising prices,” she says.

Bending Spoons has demonstrated how much financial value can be unlocked from established software businesses. Its growing portfolio suggests it has little intention of slowing down. But every acquisition brings customers whose loyalty was earned long before Bending Spoons arrived. The company’s future may depend as much on giving them reasons to stay as on finding the next business to buy.

#10440. CLEAR is giving members 5 free airport guest passes for the holidays. Here’s how to get them

Holiday travel can be stressful enough without worrying about getting everyone in your group through airport security. This year, CLEAR is introducing a new perk that could make things a little easier for members, their friends, and family.

Starting today, CLEAR members can share up to five free Holiday Guest Passes with friends and family who aren’t already members, giving them access to the company’s expedited airport security service for 14 days.

And there’s an especially useful detail: You don’t have to be traveling with someone to send them a pass. The passes are part of a broader holiday travel push from CLEAR that includes a redesigned app, new gift cards, personalized airport assistance, and the company’s biggest membership discount of the year.

How to get CLEAR’s free holiday guest passes

For the holidays, CLEAR is making guest passes available directly through its mobile app, allowing members to share them with a single tap.

“If you’re a CLEAR member, you’ll be able to open your CLEAR app, and you’ll see them, and you’ll have up to five to send to family and friends who are not members,” Campbell Millum, CLEAR’s vice president of communications, told Fast Company.

That means members can send a pass to someone traveling across the country, even if they aren’t flying together.

“If you know that your friend is traveling, if you know your mom is traveling, or a friend or family member, you can go ahead and send those, and then they can have the experience of CLEAR at what we know is the most stressful time of the year to travel,” Millum said.

Recipients will need to stop at CLEAR’s airport pods to enroll before using the service. Once enrolled, they’ll have access to CLEAR for 14 days, potentially covering both their outbound and return flights.

CLEAR’s new app helps travelers get from home to gate

Alongside the guest passes, CLEAR is introducing an upgraded app designed to help travelers navigate more than just airport security. The app now features Planning Mode and Travel Mode, which automatically adapt to different stages of a trip.

Planning Mode helps travelers prepare before leaving home, including booking a ride to the airport and calculating when to leave based on traffic conditions and their preferred airport arrival time.

Once travelers arrive at the airport, Travel Mode takes over, helping them locate CLEAR+ lanes, estimate the walk to their departure gate, and access services such as CLEAR Concierge.

The app also supports Live Activities, allowing travelers to receive real-time updates on their phone’s lock screen.

“We want to help members win the day of travel from home to gate and back again,” Millum said. “We hear all the time, and I know for myself, that travel isn’t just about the moment you get to the airport. It starts long before when you’re at home, when you’re planning, and then all the way through to when you get to your gate.”

Millum said the company wants to take some of the guesswork out of travel by bringing information and services into one place.

“We know that between your flight, the traffic, and the walk to your gate, we want the app to do the math so that you don’t have to,” he said, noting that the app uses real-time information to help travelers plan their airport arrival, rather than relying solely on historical estimates.

“We want to make sure that whenever holiday travel is already stressful because of all the unknowns, you’re [not left] asking, ‘When do I leave? Where’s my gate? How far is my gate?’” she said.

The company is also introducing gift cards, allowing customers to purchase its services for friends, family members, employees, or clients.

The busiest holiday travel days, according to CLEAR

The announcement comes as CLEAR prepares for what it expects to be a particularly busy holiday travel season.

Based on historical travel patterns, the company predicts Sunday, November 29, will be the busiest day of the season for its members, with security lines expected to be especially crowded between 5 and 7 a.m. and remain busy until 6 p.m. local time.

For Christmas, CLEAR expects Friday, December 18, to be the busiest departure day, with additional crowds anticipated on December 22 and 23. The return rush is expected to peak Sunday, December 27, with crowds beginning to ease around 5 p.m.

The predictions are based on CLEAR’s own travel patterns rather than nationwide airport passenger totals, so actual airport conditions may vary.

#10438. Ray-Ban Meta Audio review: Great specs, shame about the price

Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses attempt to curb the controversy by removing the cameras, and while they’re still an excellent product, the price makes them harder to recommend.

This has been a bit of a rollercoaster year for Meta wearables. Meta’s VR division shrank considerably earlier this year, then later announced a massively redesigned follow-up that’ll launch next year. And while Meta has debuted dozens of new smart glasses styles throughout the year that have sold quite well, the company can’t seem to get away from controversy. That’s where Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses come in.

Now, that doesn’t mean Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses aren’t worthwhile. They feature a much wider prescription range (-12 to +6) than the majority of Meta smart glasses models, which often cap out at -6 to +6. The battery life is also significantly better thanks to the lack of a camera and other improvements in the hardware. And, of course, if you want a pair of AI glasses but don’t want the camera, these are the only options from Meta.

If I were to choose between the two available models, I’d pick the Clubmaster style every time. Not only do they look better overall and feature the thinnest frames of any Meta smart glasses, but they also have substantially better nosepads that are adjustable and can be easily replaced.

The Burbank model looks just fine, but the nosepads aren’t the same, and the glasses feel more rigid overall (which I find less comfortable). Both models come in lots of colors with many different lens options, including clear, tinted, polarized, Transitions, and prescription.

Both models feature a touchpad on the outside of the right temple arm, as well as a small, circular button up top to activate Meta AI. You can alternatively use the “Hey, Meta” keywords to activate Meta AI. The button and touchpad can be disabled if you like. Only the touchpad has an alternative function, and that alternative function only controls music playback via Spotify or Amazon Music. Other Meta glasses offer far more options.

Both styles are the lightest Meta glasses available. Most Meta smart glasses with cameras weigh in around the 54g mark. Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses weigh just 44g. They’re not as light as Even Realities G2, RayNeo iO, or MemoMind One, but 44g is still considered pretty light for smart glasses.

Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses reuse the case from Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2, which looks more like a traditional Ray-Ban case rather than the foldable one that ships with Meta Ray-Ban Display or the 2026 Meta Camera Glasses. I don’t have an issue with Ray-Ban Meta Audio’s case at all, but I really enjoy the foldable one and wish it were included.

Audio playback on these is great, and while the speakers are identical to all other Meta glasses products, using them as spatial surround sound “headphones” while watching a movie with surround sound is a fantastic experience. They also have spatial audio recording and truly excellent noise cancellation thanks to the 6-mic setup.

But the lack of the newer processor from Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 means the glasses don’t support the new hearing aid function. To me, that’s a massive missed opportunity since these are audio-only glasses. When I asked Meta about it, they only said it wasn’t available on Ray-Ban Meta Audio for now, so this problem could be fixed in an upcoming update.

And that’s actually where Meta’s glasses might shine brightest: software updates. The company has been exemplary with update cadence on all of its products, and its smart glasses constantly get new, innovative features that surprise and delight. While I’m a little underwhelmed with the number of features available on these glasses today, this product will likely look quite different a year from now, a fact that’s backed up by years of Meta significantly improving product feature sets over time.

If you buy these glasses today, know that you’re mainly investing in them for the future. They’re fine enough for today’s usage, especially if you’re interested in a hands-free way to use Meta AI products like Muse or just want an open-ear way to listen to music and take phone calls, but Meta’s penchant for continually adding new features is, undoubtedly, going to be the highlight for everyone who ever buys them.

The baying of the hounds can be heard at a distance. Yesterday, Nvidia's Jensen Huang confirmed that it was indeed true that he had a romantic affair with Alice Huang (not related to the family), who U.S. intelligence services claim is a Chinese honeypot tasked with facilitating smuggling of the firm's advanced GPUs into China. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year."

Other legal firms have launched their own investigations into the recent development, with essentially the same justification: Schall, Brown & Schwartz attributes a 5.5% pre-market-trading drop to Nvidia, as does Levi & Korsinsky. The office of Frank R. Cruz mentions an 8.8% figure related to intra-day exchanging, and is interested in shareholders with $50,000 in losses. The percentage-drop figure is 5.88% premarket for Bronstein, Gewritz & Grossman.

Every investigation and suit mentioned here requires no upfront fees from complainants, as with most class-action lawsuits. The underlying condition is often that the law firms involved get a cut of whichever damages or settlements may appear at the end of the lawsuit. Some of them, like the one by Levi & Korsinsky, even aim to relieve investors who've already sold their Nvidia shares and sold them at a loss, with no minimum amount required.

#10435. A new guideline doesn’t change care

Early in my career as a neonatologist, group B streptococcus (GBS) was one of the infections we feared most. Babies who appeared healthy could become critically ill within hours or days, leaving physicians to tell parents that their newborn was suddenly fighting a life-threatening infection.

Eventually, evidence gave us a way to prevent many of those infections. Researchers found that screening pregnant women for GBS, and treating those who tested positive with antibiotics during labor could dramatically reduce transmission to newborns. Professional societies issued recommendations. But practice did not change overnight.

It took years of clearer guidelines, physician education, and standardized workflows before universal GBS screening became embedded into routine prenatal care. I spent much of my career developing and implementing evidence-based guidelines across neonatal and population health programs. That experience taught me something healthcare needs to pay more attention to today: A guideline can tell clinicians what good care looks like, but on its own it cannot make that care happen.

That matters as medicine advances faster than our healthcare system’s ability to incorporate those advances into everyday practice.

THE GAP BETWEEN EVIDENCE AND ACTION

Clinical research asks whether a diagnostic or treatment works. Implementation science asks what happens next: If we know something works, what will it take to make sure patients receive it?

GBS screening offers useful lessons. Early recommendations gave clinicians multiple approaches. Over time, guidance became more decisive and universal screening became the standard. But guidelines were only part of what changed.

Healthcare built a reliable system around them. The recommendation became a workflow. There was clear timing set for screening, a standard test, a straightforward result, and an established intervention. Responsibility for each step needed to be clear until the process became routine.

That is the lesson we should carry forward as we consider some of the most promising advances in medicine today.

GENOMIC MEDICINE IS AN IMPLEMENTATION CHALLENGE

While innovation is here, there are implementation challenges. Genomic sequencing is a good example. Evidence supporting exome and genome sequencing has expanded significantly, particularly for children with suspected genetic conditions. Clinical guidelines increasingly recognize its role in helping patients reach a diagnosis earlier.

Guidelines, though, are a leading indicator of change, not the endpoint.

Putting genomic testing into practice is more complex. For a clinician, the diagnostic journey starts with connecting subtle clinical clues to a potential hereditary etiology. What follows is a demanding progression of matching symptoms to the right test, guiding the family through pre-test choices, and deciphering complex findings into a tailored care plan.

Once a diagnosis is confirmed, it reshapes the trajectory on various levels by modifying treatments. It establishes surveillance protocols and potentially identifies at-risk relatives. Every transition, though, creates another opportunity for adoption to break down.

Meanwhile, operational friction looms over the entire path. Insurance roadblocks and limited access to specialized genetics colleagues, along with cumbersome documentation routines often overshadow the clinical merits. Even the strongest guidelines will fail to shift behavior when the everyday reality makes acting on them nearly impossible.

CLOSE THE GAP BETWEEN GUIDELINES AND PRACTICE

If we want medical innovation to reach patients, we need to design for implementation from the beginning. Can the right patient be identified easily? Does the clinician know when testing is appropriate? Is ordering simple? Is coverage predictable? Can the result be understood and acted upon? Is it clear who owns the next step?

And critically, can the process work not only at leading academic medical centers with deep specialty resources, but in the places where most patients actually receive care?

Today, we have tools that can accelerate this transition. Clinical decision support can help identify patients who may benefit from testing. Digital ordering can reduce administrative burden. AI can help clinicians navigate complex information. Telehealth can extend access to genetics expertise.

But the goal should be to remove the friction between what medicine knows and what clinicians can realistically do.

WE BUILD THE STANDARD OF CARE

Healthcare often talks about achieving standard of care as though it happens when enough evidence accumulates or a professional society updates its recommendations. My experience has taught me to think about it differently.

A true standard of care exists when the right care happens reliably across physicians, health systems, geographies, and patient populations without requiring extraordinary effort from the clinician or patient. Guidelines are essential, but they have to be translated into coverage and workflows. They need to be included in education and clinician confidence, as well as provide access.

The history of GBS screening shows us that evidence can transform medicine, but only when we build the systems that allow clinicians to act on it. Genomic medicine is a more complex implementation challenge, but the lesson is the same.

We have spent decades getting better at discovering what works in medicine. Now we need to become just as good at making it work in the real world.

Linda Genen, MD, MPH, is chief medical officer at GeneDx.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When developing a website, developers often rely on CSS classes to style buttons, forms, navigation elements, and other interface components. This approach works well, but some situations require styles to depend on an element's HTML attributes rather than additional class names.

CSS attribute selectors provide a practical solution. They allow developers to target elements based on whether an attribute exists, what value it contains, or whether its value matches a particular pattern. Used carefully, they can simplify styling and make reusable components easier to maintain.

An attribute selector targets an HTML element using square brackets. For example, a developer can select every input field that has a required attribute:

This rule applies to inputs with the required attribute, regardless of their input type.

Developers can also target a specific attribute value:

This is useful when different input types need different visual treatments without introducing additional classes into the HTML.

Forms are a practical place to apply attribute selectors because HTML already provides attributes that describe how individual fields behave.

Consider a registration form containing email, password, and telephone fields. Each input can be styled according to its purpose:

The CSS can target these fields independently:

This approach keeps the markup descriptive while allowing the stylesheet to respond to the attributes already present in the document.

One important distinction is that required indicates a validation requirement, while :invalid represents an input's current validity state. These should not be treated as interchangeable.

CSS provides several matching operators that help developers target more specific attribute values.

These operators can be useful when working with links, downloadable files, language attributes, and reusable components.

For example, a website might want to distinguish PDF downloads from ordinary navigation links:

This adds a small visual indicator to links whose URLs end in .pdf.

Attribute selectors can also help identify links with different destinations or behaviors.

For example, external links that use HTTPS can receive a subtle visual indicator:

However, matching an HTTPS URL does not necessarily prove that a link points to an external website. Internal links can also use HTTPS, so developers should consider the actual navigation requirements before applying special styling.

For more examples of selector combinations and matching rules, SitePoint's guide to CSS Attribute Selectors provides a useful reference.

Although attribute selectors are flexible, they should not replace every class-based styling decision.

A selector such as [class*="button"] can match unintended elements if their class names happen to contain the same text. Similarly, broad attribute rules may affect components that were not originally intended to receive those styles.

For predictable results, use exact attribute matching whenever possible and prefer descriptive classes for major component styling.

Developers should also remember that CSS selectors only control presentation. They do not replace JavaScript validation, server-side security checks, or proper HTML semantics.

The MDN documentation on attribute selectors provides further details about selector syntax, matching behavior, and supported operators.

Before adding attribute selectors to a large stylesheet, inspect the affected elements using browser developer tools.

Check whether the selector matches the intended elements.

Test fields with different attribute values.

Verify disabled, required, and invalid form states.

Check navigation links and downloadable files.

Test the layout on mobile and desktop screens.

Review whether existing component styles are being unintentionally overridden.

This process helps identify unexpected matches before they affect the production interface.

CSS attribute selectors give developers another way to create flexible and maintainable interfaces without adding unnecessary classes to every HTML element.

They are particularly useful for form styling, link identification, and components that already contain meaningful HTML attributes. By choosing precise selectors, understanding matching operators, and testing changes before deployment, developers can use this feature to write cleaner CSS while keeping their markup descriptive and organized.

#10431. The best AI lab in business is not for sale—you already own it

The last time every client wanted to talk about the same thing at the same time, it was Y2K. It is happening again with AI, but with a key difference. This time, the money is outpacing the understanding.

From the internet to cloud to mobile, each technology wave follows the same pattern. Companies rush in and treat adoption as a what question, while it should be a who question.

We lead firms with different specialties. BDO’s is assurance, tax, and advisory; Gagen MacDonald’s specialty is people-centered change. Working together on BDO’s AI transformation confirmed what we both see with organizations: Technology creates the possibility of transformation, but people determine whether it succeeds.

WHY THE RETURNS AREN’T SHOWING UP

As boards set their 2027 budgets, one question will follow AI spending into nearly every conversation: Why isn’t it showing up in our results? Intelligence platform AI4SP found that for the first half of 2026, 76% of enterprise AI initiatives struggled to show return on investment, while in 2025, Gartner projected that more than 40% of agentic AI projects would be canceled by the end of 2027.

The reflex is to write a bigger check for a more capable platform. But buying more of what companies have struggled to turn into value cannot be the fix.

We believe most firms treat AI as a technology purchase. We treat it as a people transformation. Hand the best tools in the world to people who have no reason to care, and you have bought expensive software nobody uses.

But the response should not be a top-down mandate nor a pure grassroots initiative. At BDO, we call it guided grassroots: Leadership sets the direction, and the people closest to the work build the solutions. We are equipping and encouraging each of BDO’s 14,000-plus team members to find where AI belongs in their work, within parameters and guardrails.

LISTEN BEFORE YOU SPEND

Before we spend big on anything new at BDO, we listen. Our technology partner ran an anonymous diagnostic that nearly 3,500 colleagues answered in April and May. The results showed that 87% were already using AI, and more than 11,000 ideas came back for how our professionals could use AI to improve their work and processes.

Interestingly, almost nobody asked for an additional or different platform. They asked for help from AI with the many small things that rob people of time that could be spent on client relationships, developing their teams, and deep work. This proved the innovation engine already existed. It now needed structure, support, and governance to scale.

MAKE IT VISIBLE, THEN SCALE IT

BDO’s AI champions, embedded across the firm, help colleagues find useful applications, experiment within guardrails, and share what works, so ideas spread sideways. A firm-wide dashboard makes the work visible. It details which agents are in use, who built them, and who else relies on them.

At BDO, the rule is simple. Our people build it, we measure business impact, and we scale what works. Before our first formal training session, more than 600 team members had already built over 1,200 working agents. Two weeks after training an initial group of champions, the number of agents built had increased by roughly 80%, and the number of builders had grown by more than 50%.

To contextualize those numbers, consider when BDO’s brand language changes, which often happens twice a year. Updating nearly 2,000 design files used to take 20 people close to a month. Emma, one of our creative professionals, used AI to shape an automation that updates the designs in about a day. It only took one person. Encouragingly, the other 19 employees are still on that team. The month they used to lose to rework now goes back into the creative work they were hired to do.

Finding meaningful ways to help people effectively use AI is the first challenge. Keeping active what people build is another. Our technology partner’s research finds that without the internal capacity to continually maintain and improve agents, more than 60% of users stop engaging with them within three months. An agent creates value as people continue to use it, which means organizations need the internal capacity to sustain and improve what they build.

HOW BOARDS SHOULD LOOK AT IT

We do not recommend uncontrolled adoption. Leaders decide which tools people use, what information those tools can reach, and how to verify outputs. BDO’s first practice-wide agent is for quality checks. It flags what a reviewer should look at and preserves human judgment and decision-making authority.

As boards ask where the returns are, they should consider whether they have built an organization capable of discovering what AI is good for and then scaling what they find.

Outside providers will remain essential for models, infrastructure, and technical expertise. But they equip the lab. They are not the lab. The best AI lab in business? You already own it.

Maril Gagen MacDonald is the founder and CEO of Gagen MacDonald. Matthew Becker is the chief executive officer of BDO USA.
