An Oslo rooftop, about 80 watts, and a hand-aimed antenna were enough to reach orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Oslo radio amateur group, working with Tanagra Space, got a European Space Agency satellite to recognize and launch the 1993 game Doom after catching the word in a voice command sent over the 23 cm band. It took seven attempts, shared with a group in Poland, and the command finally got through on the last two, on the same day in late July. The satellite “understood its assignment,” with the help of a matcher after the 27 MB onboard speech model transcribed the audio, returning a postcard with details of the launch.

The satellite, named OPS-SAT PRETTY and flying under the ESA’s OPS-SAT Space Lab program for outside experiments, ran the game in an experiment punningly called PRETTY DOOMed. Doom ran on a different satellite, the OPS-SAT-1, in 2023, but this time is different, as the game was launched with a voice command.

The radio club sending the command in question is LA4O, of the Norwegian Radio Relay League, hams transmitting as part of the experiment. The club’s signal went over 1296 MHz narrowband FM at about 80 W, indicated, using an Icom IC-9700 radio and a Wimo helix antenna at 15.1 dBi, directed by hand. As for the voice, Run 6, the morning pass, used a looped synthesized voice from a keyer, with three of six captures detecting the command. Run 7, the evening pass, used a live operator at a microphone, with one of five usable captures detecting it.

The live operator’s command was “LIMA ALFA FOUR OSCAR, PRETTY PLAY DOOM DOOM DOOM, PRETTY PLAY DOOM DOOM DOOM.” The call sign is for legal identification.

On board the satellite, the voice is transcribed by a 27 MB quantized English speech-recognition model, picked because it could fit the satellite’s limited computer. The voice was handled by software-defined radio (SDR), which was able to narrow in on the voice and demodulate the source for the speech model. Tuning and demodulating a signal is usually handled by fixed circuits, but using software has the advantage of being mutable with an uploaded update. The voice used this time “was only the test signal,” project lead Georges Labrèche said, and the same setup could handle other things with a new model.

The live-voice transcript caught “AND FAR BRIEFLY PLAYING DOOM STEAM DOOM PRECIPATED” with two exact DOOM matches, although one DOOM is enough. Morning detections passed only on fuzzy tolerance with transcripts such as “PLAY DOON.” The achievement is less on the understood side and more about differentiating a voice and a specific command out of the noise in orbit.

This can be an iffy business, which is one reason it took seven runs, and being able to update proved useful. The spacecraft heard LA4O, but the output was mostly static, because about 170 kHz reached the FM discriminator for a signal of about ±5 kHz. Offline analysis brought a fix: find the peak within ±100 kHz, shift to baseband, low-pass, and decimate before demodulation. It’s effectively like tuning a car radio to a specific station.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Tanagra then reproduced the fix and was able to remove a redundant audio filter. Delivery of the fix took about a week, although the Oslo group’s effort took 59 days and about 7,200 NOK (about $770), pizza included.

Tanagra proposes repeat runs that keep the original data and send it back down to Earth, so the researchers can test the live-voice result properly. Better detection may be possible with larger speech models, too, which the team could test on the ground first. Labrèche says the team has demonstrated “a satellite that can listen to any type of radio signal.” Hopefully, the setup can one day detect “mayday” calls and even radio bursts from space.

#10427. Jensen Huang resigns: Nvidia shares tumble even further after scandal-ridden CEO replaced with interim boss

Update: Thursday, 9:15 a.m. ET:

Jensen Huang has resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia, the company’s board of directors announced on Thursday.

The move caps a dramatic week for one of the most influential titans of tech, who had become embroiled in scandals surrounding two extramarital affairs, one with an alleged spy and another with a subordinate.

Huang’s resignation is effective immediately.

Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia’s EVP and CFO, has agreed to serve as Interim CEO until a permanent replacement can be found, Nvidia said. The company’s lack of a cohesive succession plan has caused concern among analysts and investors alike.

Premarket shares of Nvidia Corp. (Nasdaq: NVDA) fell even further on Thursday morning following the news of Huang’s departure.

As of this writing, the stock is down almost 13% in premarket trading. That’s in addition to an 11.33.% decline over the last five trading sessions.

This story is developing…

Original story appears below:

Shares of Nvidia Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA) are once again sinking in premarket trading this morning after reports yesterday that the company’s board has convened to discuss whether to oust its embattled cofounder and CEO, Jensen Huang.

As of this writing, NVDA shares are down more than 7% in premarket trading, mainly due to uncertainty over Huang’s fate.

But several Wall Street analysts worry that Nvidia’s lack of a known succession plan could weigh on the stock’s price for a long time. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

This week started out bad for Nvidia, and yesterday things got worse.

On Sunday, CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe could be a Chinese spy. That raised severe national security concerns and led to a steep sell-off in NVDA stock.

However, at the time, Nvidia’s board released a statement saying it still had “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

In other words: it was a scandal, but the board backed its CEO (and said it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised).

But things got worse yesterday.

That’s when The Wall Street Journal revealed that Nvidia’s board was meeting to determine whether to oust Huang. What changed? News broke of an alleged second affair that Huang had had, this time with a subordinate who works at Nvidia.

At this time, Huang’s fate remains unknown. But it’s precisely that uncertainty—and what comes next if he is ousted—that has Wall Street fearing for NVDA stock.

Nvidia has no publicly known succession plan

One of the greatest periods of anxiety and uncertainty for employees and investors is when a company changes leadership. 

If the old leader was good, can the new one measure up? Will the new leader change tack? Will the bottom line be impacted? Will the corporate environment change? What about employee morale and productivity?

Leadership changes often bring these kinds of questions, even in ideal situations, when a CEO change has been telegraphed long in advance (as was done with Apple’s CEO transition earlier this year).

But when a CEO change happens on short notice, especially when a scandal is driving it—and the company has no known succession plans in place—that really freaks investors out.

And that’s exactly why Nvidia stock is falling so much this morning.

The company has no known succession plans for who will take over when Huang leaves the CEO role. That only adds to the uncertainty now. It’s not only: Will he be fired? It’s: Who can successfully run one of the world’s most valuable and economically important companies if Huang is ousted?

Who can replace Huang as Nvidia CEO?

It should be noted that Nvidia may have a secret succession plan in place that the company has never publicly disclosed. But if they did, the board would likely have acknowledged the plan—or at least its existence —given the uncertainty of Huang’s fate.

Regardless of whether a plan is in place, if Huang were to be ousted, Nvidia has two options for replacing him: find a new CEO from within Nvidia, or look outside. 

It’s impossible to predict which external person the company would select as the new CEO, but someone with a deep understanding of AI or chip design would be likely. 

If Nvidia looks inside, there are some obvious candidates, based on their positions at the company:

  • Colette Kress: the company’s chief financial officer.
  • Ian Buck: VP of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing
  • Michael Kagan: the company’s chief technology officer

CNBC reports that Citi analysts Atif Malik and Papa Sylla think Kress is a likely interim option while Nvidia searches for a permanent successor.

Morningstar says that if Nvidia recruits internally, Buck “strikes us as a logical successor to Jensen Huang” and “is well known to outside investors.”

But the fact of the matter is, for now, no one knows who would replace Huang.

Nvidia stock turns negative for the year

All this uncertainty is weighing on NVDA stock. As of this writing, Nvidia shares are down nearly 7.5% in premarket trading, bringing their five-day loss to over 13%—a staggering amount for a company that many see as the backbone of the AI economy.

Many investors fear worse times for NVDA ahead because of the scandal. The company is already being sued by shareholders, and a series of congressional investigations is likely.

Then the ever-present question remains: Who leads Nvidia if its visionary CEO is forced out?

“Right now, Nvidia doesn’t have [a Tim Cook to Steve Jobs-type] person in place, so it’s going to be a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with . . . all kinds of interrogations, or they’re going to have to move on from him,” Questar Capital Partners’ Richard Reyle noted to CNBC, “and that’s just going to make the stock uninvestable.”

Uninvestable or not, the company’s share price has fallen more than 33% since its all-time high above $239 in early October, when Nvidia was valued at more than $5.7 trillion—the most valuable public company in history. 

Today, post-Huang scandal, the company’s valuation is down to less than $4.2 trillion.

(Disclosure: Morningstar is owned by Joe Mansueto, owner of Fast Company parent Mansueto Ventures.)

Backend infrastructure failures included hardcoded, user-visible administrator credentials.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Before proceeding further, we'd like to advise our dear reader to sit down and perhaps grab a helmet, for this post will elicit quite a few face-palms and forehead-slaps. Two security researchers joined forces and, during early 2026, managed to hack the vehicle connectivity backend infrastructure of two automakers, managing to remotely open the doors on any of their net-connected cars and start their engines across multiple world regions.

The vulnerabilities were quickly fixed, and they pertained to a handful of belief-begging security issues with multiple server APIs that their respective mobile applications use. Furthermore, although remotely opening the cars and starting them were the most concerning bits, the vulnerabilities also exposed the vehicles' location, mileage, fuel, range, door states, and the customers' personal information.

The white-hat hacking duo isn't disclosing the name of the impacted automakers, but they managed to get access to Automaker #1's U.S. vehicles, while vehicles from Automaker #2 were susceptible to unplanned lock disengagement in Australia, the U.S., and Canada. As far as we can tell by visual inspection alone, the second firm may be Toyota, as the hack demonstration video appears to depict a RAV4 SUV.

Both affected automakers use ForgeRock's authentication and authorization services, though with the one small exception, the vulnerabilities found by Shubham Shah and Sam Curry pertained to poor implementations and security practices. One of their writeups goes over the ForgeRock-related affairs in detail for both companies, while Shah's article discusses the specifics on automaker #2 and their Australian connected-car infrastructure.

Shah first decompiled the company's Android application and found network calls to a telematics subdomain, quickly finding an "admintool" location containing a "TEST HARNESS" page with a login prompt. If you haven't been keeping track by now, the first problem is that this endpoint is reachable from the internet at large. But what really piqued Shah's interest was problem #2: a bundle of JavaScript code that should have been stripped of any unnecessary cruft actually contained the code for the backend's entire functionality, providing a map for further shenanigans.

This alone was enough to grant Shah the ability to pull up customer information with API keys that were hard-coded into said JavaScript. After some careful chaining of requests and connecting a license plate to a VIN with publicly available info, he connected that to a customer and found their email. At this point, the team noticed that the automaker was using ForgeRock's authentication mechanisms, and spent "a couple weeks" finding how they were used.

And this is also where they assess that the easiest path to victory is managing to mint an access token for any user, a task made way easier by the "cursed" JavaScript bundle they found at an endpoint containing hard-coded administrator credentials. These were likely meant for the staging environment, but the duo estimated, correctly, that they could be leveraged nevertheless.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

At this point, they ran into the WAF in front of the service. A Web Application Firewall is similar to a network firewall, but instead of working with IPs and ports, it considers endpoints (URLs) and the requirements to access them. The researchers hypothesize that although it's a good and standard practice, the WAF was put in place because of how bad things were underneath.

And they were right. The app decompilation had revealed a "pinService", and Shah found that it was accessible through the WAF. From thereon, they found "getUser", and correctly guessed that they could retrieve users' information with their email, phone, and ID. Remember those admin credentials? They came in handy, revealing the users' password hashes, but as these were SHA-512, cracking them was unfeasible.

At this point, they let GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra loose to brute-force path names, and found an unprotected one that ultimately let them overwrite any user's password, partially enabling taking over their accounts. However, there was still MFA to contend with.

As it turns out, even that too was misconfigured, as the Australian environment would let users skip MFA entirely. With some judicious token shuffling across endpoints and the mobile app, they eventually could mint access tokens, letting them fully impersonate any user account... and unlock their cars. Then, it was as simple as sending out an API request for the "door-unlock" command, and sure enough, the test car promptly opened.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

#10423. Cheddar cheese is being recalled in 12 states due to Listeria fears: Avoid these Family Farmstead Dairy products

Listeria monocytogenes outbreaks continue to spark food recalls across the country.

This time it’s Family Farmstead Dairy, which has recalled all of its cheddar cheese products due to a potential listeria contamination, according to a notice posted by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

“This action is being taken as part of our ongoing commitment to continuous improvement and product excellence,” Family Farmstead Dairy stated in the recall. “The company remains committed to producing safe, high-quality dairy products and maintaining the trust of the communities it serves.”

The FDA announcement comes less than a month after the Worcester, New York, company recalled some of its raw cheddar products due to potential E. Coli O26:H11 and O45:H2 contamination. 

Here’s what you need to know about the latest Family Farmstead Dairy recall. 

What products are affected?

The recall is for two Family Farmstead brand cheddar cheeses. Here’s all the information you need to identify them:

Raw Mild Cheddar, 8oz, plastic wrapped

  • All lot codes dated October 16, 2027 or sooner

Raw Sharp Cheddar, 8oz, plastic wrapped

  • All lot codes dated October 16, 2027 or sooner

Where and when was the product sold?

Right now, we don’t know exactly when or in which stores the recalled cheddar cheeses were sold. All we know is which states they were distributed in:

  • Connecticut
  • Delaware
  • Massachusetts 
  • New Hampshire
  • New Jersey
  • New York
  • Pennsylvania
  • Rhode Island
  • Tennessee
  • Vermont
  • Virginia 
  • West Virginia

What should I do if I have this product? 

You can either return the impacted cheese to your point of purchase or contact Family Farmstead Dairy for assistance. The company is available at customerservice@familyfarmsteaddairy.com or (607) 397-4044 from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET, Monday to Friday. 

What listeria symptoms should I look out for? 

Listeria is an organism that can cause sickness in people of all ages. Healthy individuals exposed to listeria will likely experience short-term symptoms including:

  • Abdominal pain
  • Diarrhea 
  • High fever
  • Severe headache
  • Stiffness

A listeria infection during pregnancy can lead to miscarriages or stillbirths.

Young people, elderly individuals, and anyone with a weakened immune system are at risk of more serious or even fatal results.

#10421. How to Get a YouTube API Key and Use the Data API (2026)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

You need a YouTube API key the moment your app has to read anything from YouTube: a video's length, its view count, a channel's latest uploads. Getting one takes about five minutes. Using it well takes a little longer, because YouTube changed how its quota works in June 2026, and plenty of guides still describe the old rules.

In this guide we'll get a key, lock it down and test it. Then we'll use it from Node.js for three real jobs: adding up the length of a playlist, listing a channel's videos without spending a search, and estimating what a video earned. Along the way we'll cover what the YouTube API costs (nothing), how the 2026 quota works, and the errors you're most likely to hit.

A YouTube API key identifies your project to the YouTube Data API v3. With just a key, you can read public data:

A key isn't enough for anything that touches someone's account. Uploading videos, editing playlists or reading private data needs OAuth 2.0, where the user signs in and grants your app access.

You'll need a Google account. The YouTube Data API is free, so there's nothing to pay for.

The restrictions matter more than they look. A key is just a string in a URL, and anyone who copies an unrestricted one can spend your daily quota for you. With an API restriction, the key is useless for other Google APIs. With an application restriction, it only works from your server or your site. Changes to restrictions can take up to five minutes to apply, so don't panic if a request fails straight after you save.

Before writing any code, check the key with a single request. This one asks for the first video ever uploaded to YouTube, and uses the fields parameter to trim the response down to four values:

That request cost 1 unit of your daily quota, which brings us to the question everyone asks.

Yes. There's no charge per request and no paid plan. Instead you get a daily quota, and since June 1, 2026 it's split into separate buckets:

Google's quota calculator lists the cost of every method. Quotas reset at midnight Pacific Time. Every request costs at least 1 unit, including requests that fail, so a retry loop around a broken call can use up a day's quota on its own.

If you've read older guides, search is the big change. A search used to cost 100 units out of the same 10,000, so 100 searches emptied your whole day. Uploads were worse still, at about 1,600 units each until December 2025. Now both have their own buckets, and the 10,000 units are left for everything else.

To give you a feel for what 10,000 units buys, here's what each example in this guide costs:

You can't pay for more. To go above the defaults, fill in the YouTube API Services Audit and Quota Extension Form, which is linked from Google's page on quota and compliance audits. YouTube first audits your project to check it follows the YouTube API Services Terms of Service, then someone from the API team gets back to you. Google doesn't give a timeline, so apply well before you need the extra quota.

Most projects never need to. The rest of this guide is about getting a lot done with very few units.

The examples need Node.js 20.6 or later, for the built-in fetch and the --env-file flag. There are no packages to install. Make a folder with a .env file in it:

Every example imports one small helper. It builds the URL, adds your key and turns API errors into readable messages:

Run any example with node --env-file=.env followed by the file name.

YouTube doesn't tell you how long a playlist is. To work it out, you need two methods:

Durations come back in ISO 8601 format. PT15M33S is 15 minutes 33 seconds, PT1H2M3S adds an hour, and a stream longer than a day looks like P1DT2H3M4S. The toSeconds() function below handles all three.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Full Courses in One Video playlist:

That's 184 hours of courses for 4 units of quota. Private and deleted videos still show up in a playlist's items, but videos.list doesn't return them, which is why the script prints "52 of 52 videos available". On a playlist with removed videos, the two numbers will differ.

This is the core of the free YouTube playlist length calculator I built on createthat.ai. The live version adds a target time box that works out the speed you need to finish by a deadline, and it accepts channel, video and Shorts links as well as playlists.

The obvious way to find a channel's videos is to search for them. Don't: search is now capped at 100 calls a day, and it isn't built to list everything a channel has posted. Every channel has an uploads playlist instead, and you can reach it in two cheap calls:

Two units, and none of your 100 daily searches. To get every upload rather than the newest five, page through the playlist with the same pageToken loop as Example 1.

videos.list with part=statistics returns a video's view, like and comment counts. Dislike counts have been private since December 2021 and favoriteCount is always 0, so don't build anything on those. The script also copes with a missing like or comment count, which you'll see on some videos.

This time the fields parameter trims the response to the values we use. That makes the response smaller, but it doesn't change the cost: the call is 1 unit either way.

Here it is on freeCodeCamp's Learn Python full course, one of the most-watched videos in that playlist:

Treat the last line as a rough range, not an answer. The Data API doesn't share anyone's revenue, so any estimate is views multiplied by an RPM: what a creator keeps per 1,000 views. RPM moves a lot with the topic and where the viewers live, and the estimate assumes the video shows ads, which not every channel does.

And sometimes you don't need an API at all. When I built a font tester, I needed a list of Google Fonts. The Google Fonts Developer API would have meant a key and a call on every visit, for a list that barely changes. Instead I generated a file of the 500 most popular fonts once, from Google's public font metadata, and the page loads it like any other file. No key, no quota and nothing to fail.

When a call fails, the response's error.message and error.details[0].reason tell you why. These are the ones you'll see most:

For the invalid key error, the full response looks like this:

Yes. Creating a key and calling the YouTube Data API costs nothing. You're limited by the daily quota instead, and there's no paid tier: more quota comes through an audit.

In the Google Cloud console, select your project and go to APIs & Services > Credentials. Your keys are listed under API keys, with a Show key option next to each one.

It works, but anyone can read the key from your page. If you do it, restrict the key to your website and to the YouTube Data API v3. A small server route that calls the API for you is safer, and it gives you somewhere to cache results.

By default, 100 searches, 100 uploads and 10,000 units for everything else. Most reads cost 1 unit and videos.list takes 50 IDs per call, so that's enough for the details of up to 500,000 videos a day.

Getting a YouTube API key is the easy part: one project, one API to enable, one key and two restrictions. The 2026 quota is generous if you work with it:

All three examples together cost 7 units, out of 10,000. From here, try commentThreads.list to pull a video's comments 100 at a time, or extend Example 2 to page through a channel's entire upload history and add it all up with the code from Example 1.

Seagate wants you to side-load an SSD in its latest external hard drive.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's old is new again. Seagate started adding faster flash-based storage to its hard drives in 2010, when solid-state storage was prohibitively expensive. And now that SSDs are stupid-expensive again (thanks, AI hyperscaler demand) the hard drive maker is offering up another hybrid drive, of sorts, with the Firecuda Forge.

Available in 8TB and 20TB capacities, the Forge is an external hard drive that requires that you bring and install your own SSD. That's right, the drive won't work unless you partially disassemble and install your own M.2 2280 SSD, which mounts in the side of the enclosure. 1TB drives with DRAM are recommended. Performance maxes out at PCIe Gen3 drives; newer, faster, and roomier SSDs are supported, but won't improve performance. The Firecuda Forge only has a mounting point for 2280-length drives, and while drives that are less than 1TB are supported, that means less room for frequently used files, so "performance may be reduced."

Interestingly, Seagate sent us a 2TB FireCuda 530R SSD to test with the Forge hard drive, which is both faster (PCIe 4.0) and more spacious than what the company says you should pair with its hard drive. The list of SSD that Seagate has officially qualified to work with the Firecuda Forge is also pretty sparse, including just three other drives: Samsung's 990 Pro, WD/Sandisk SN850X/GX Pro 850X, and the WD/SanDisk SN710/GX7100.

We only received a review sample a few days before launch, and haven't yet had a chance to put the FireCuda Forge through its paces for a full review. But I was impressed that, after I installed the SSD and plugged the drive in, it just showed up in Windows 11 as an 8TB drive. (The company says it also works with macOS 26 and later). There was no software setup involved, and Seagate says you can even remove and upgrade the hard drive to something roomier down the line. Seagate calls the "product architecture" that handles unifying and data handling between the spinning platter drive and the SSD "Alkemi," and says it combines "onboard processing" with the hard drive and the user-supplied SSD to "prioritize active data without requiring users to manually manage separate drives."

Seagate says Alkemi observes workloads and gives priority to currently relevant or often-used data, that it adapts over time to user behavior, and describes it as an "on-device device dynamic caching and workload-aware data-prioritization technology." That sounds pretty similar to the SSD caching used on hybrid drives of the early 2010s, although with up to 1TB of fast SSD storage, you're getting a much bigger fast data pool than those drives of the past, which often made do with 4-16GB.

Interestingly, Seagate says that machine learning is a part of what Alkemi does, but repeatedly points out in its review materials that it is not using generative AI. It's likely the company is worried about customers connecting the many reported instances of LLMs and agents deleting data with this new product. I can understand why Seagate would want to distance its hybrid storage tech from reports of catastrophic data deletion.

Getting past the somewhat odd-feeling aspect of having to crack open an external drive right out of the box and install another drive into it in order for it to work, the process was pretty painless. You have to remove four screws from the bottom (with a tiny included hex-bit driver) to get the outer shell off the FireCuda Forge. From there, the M.2 drive bay is clearly visible on the side. If you want to remove six more hex screws, you can also pop out the hard drive for future upgrades. But for now, we're just going to install an M.2 SSD.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

SSD installation is pretty much the same as putting one of these drives in any laptop or motherboard. Though you'll need a tool; the drive requires a a tiny screw and Seagate does not include a suitable Phillips head screwdriver. The drive bay is somewhat recessed, and there are two thick thermal pads included in the box that should ensure the drive makes contact with both the inner edge of the bay and the external shroud.

This should provide some heat dissipation, but these surfaces are all's plastic, with only a foil layer on the outer shroud to draw some of the drive's heat away from the SSD itself. This is probably fine for most bursty game and creative workloads. But this design does not feel ideal for workloads that hit the drive consistently for hours on end. During our testing, the edge of the drive where the SSD is installed got noticeably warmer than the rest of the enclosure, but it didn't get hot.

In terms of design, the FireCuda Forge looks very similar to the FireCuda X Vault HDD we looked at earlier this year, complete with some gamer-friendly RGB lighting. The primary physical difference is that you'll need the supplied USB-C cable and external power adapter to use the Forge, while the X Vault only has a USB-C port. Presumably, powering both a 3.5-inch hard drive and an M.2 SSD draws too much power for most (or at least some) USB-C ports. I still would love for drives like this to be able to run off of one single cable, though, which was my favorite feature of the X Vault hard drive.

We only received the FireCuda Forge a couple of working days before its announcement. But we were able to run some benchmarks with the Forge drive and a 530R SSD that Seagate provided, and saw some interesting results. The Forge's USB-C connection is USB4, and Seagate's performance claims are up to 2,500 MB/s read and 2,000 MB/s write. That's obviously much faster than a hard drive, but you're also going to be sacrificing the speed of the SSD you're dropping into this drive — especially if it's a PCIe 4.0 SSD.

PCMark 10 is a trace-based benchmark that uses a wide-ranging set of real-world traces from popular applications and everyday tasks to measure the performance of storage devices.

On this synthetic test, Seagate's Forge beats recent traditional hard drives (and the slowest external SSD we've tested, Samsung's T5). But Kingston's fast flash drive does better, as does Sandisk's Desk Drive, which nearly doubles the score of the Forge, which isn't surprising given it's a full-fledged external SSD.

We use the DiskBench storage benchmarking tool to test file transfer performance with a custom 50GB dataset. We copy 4,617 files (images, videos, and software ISO files) to a folder on the test drive (write). Then, after leaving the system idle for five minutes, we run the same test in reverse, moving the test folder to a different location on our PCIe 4.0 testing drive.

Here , we see the Forge drive easily beating the spinning-platter-only drives and Samsung's T5 Evo on writes, only falling to the SanDisk Desk Drive desktop SSD. But on reads, the Forge leads by the pack.

CrystalDiskMark (CDM) is a free and easy-to-run storage benchmarking tool that SSD companies commonly use to assign performance specifications to their products. It gives us insight into how each device handles different file sizes. We run this test at its default settings.

Last up (for now), CrystalDiskMark proves the Forge does benefit significantly from its USB4 interface, with its performance on sequential reads and writes jumping well ahead of everything else on our chart — because all other drives here top out at 10 Gbps. There are, of course, faster external SSDs (like Samsung's recent P9). But at 8TB, solid-state options are generally more expensive, and faster external SSDs at 8TB are much more expensive. And of course, 20TB external SSDs aren't really an option, at least in the consumer drive space.

The whole reason a product like the Seagate Forge exists is because SSDs are expensive. The problem is, hard drives have faced similar price jumps due to demand. And Seagate says the 8TB Forge will launch at $699 for the 8TB drive, and $899 for the 20TB option. That's a lot of money for a drive you need to also put your own M.2 SSD into for it to function.

We'll also need to do more testing with things like game load times before passing judgment on the FireCuda Forge. But it likely makes much more sense in the 20TB capacity, where no single-drive consumer SSD-based option exists. At 8TB, there are options like SanDisk's Desk drive, which has a slower 10GBps interface, but is a full-fledged SSD, rather than a hard drive with some fast SSD cache. Surprisingly, that Sandisk drive is still on sale for $999. And unless you happen to have an old M.2 SSD lying around to install into the Forge, its price, including the SSD it needs to function, isn't going to be far off traditional solid-state options.

#10416. How advertising machines broke the attention economy

In 2016, TV advertising was in trouble. People were canceling their cable subscriptions by the millions, ratings were slipping, and advertisers were pouring billions of dollars into digital platforms that promised bigger audiences than TV at a much lower cost.

That April, Buzzfeed broadcast a live stream of two staffers in white coats and safety goggles wrapping rubber bands around a watermelon. The tension mounted as the rubber bands piled up, one at a time, hundreds and hundreds of them, squeezing the watermelon until it began to buckle. When it finally burst, sending pulp flying and its hosts shrieking, the live stream had been viewed more than 3 million times. CNBC called it the future of television.

Except it wasn’t. There was no way to tell how much of the audience actually watched the spectacle, or only watched it for a few seconds. The video may have simply run on autoplay as they scrolled past. But for advertisers, every three-second “view” counted as an impression, which was the industry’s basic unit of value.

Advertising had always been the business of attention. But attention is finite. There are only 24 hours in a day, and people can look at only so many things at once. But the algorithms that controlled digital advertising weren’t built to reflect that reality. They were given an incentive: maximize ad revenue. So they learned to produce and promote whatever generated the most impressions. An impression was counted each time an ad, or the content around it, appeared on a screen for a few seconds, whether or not anyone actually noticed it.

When the algorithms ran short of real attention to sell, they expanded into areas that required no attention at all: intercepting demand that already existed and claiming credit for purchases people would have made anyway. That set off a snowball effect. The supply of ad inventory exploded. The result was a flood of cheap, low-quality impressions—a subprime market for human attention.  As supply soared, prices fell for every seller of advertising. Never mind that TV commercials were graded differently. Scrolling past an exploding watermelon on your phone was treated the same way as watching every minute of a prime-time drama or a World Series game.

A vicious cycle

As television was forced to compete on digital’s terms, networks ran more minutes of advertising, which made the viewing experience worse and probably played a role in pushing even more viewers toward streaming and ad-free platforms. It was a vicious cycle. The less attention was worth, the more “impressions” the industry had to manufacture to make up the difference.

As traditional TV ads lost value, some networks experimented with cutting ad loads and rethinking the commercial break altogether. At the time, Jonathan was in charge of advertising at Fox Networks Group, and we experimented with a bunch of new formats: six-second spots, premium slots at the start and end of commercial breaks and even single-sponsor streams with minimal interruptions. Other networks pursued their own versions of the same idea, promising viewers fewer, better ads and offering advertisers more engaged audiences. These new formats provided a better value exchange for viewers’ attention. But they were a hard sell. Buyers asked why six seconds should cost more than 30. The real estate and retail industries valued placement and scarcity, but when it came to the advertising market, brands wanted volume. Real change required advertisers to let their agencies take risks and most wouldn’t do it.

A decade later, the stakes are even higher. There are still only 24 hours in a day, but artificial intelligence can now generate an unlimited supply of content. Feeds are filling up with AI-generated videos, and platforms are automating every step of advertising, from writing an ad to targeting the audience to placing the buy. There are now even ads inside AI assistants. ChatGPT says it’s on track to generate $1 billion in annual ad revenue, and more than 100,000 advertisers are running campaigns on the platform.

The risk is that an endless supply of content chasing a finite supply of attention will make each impression cheaper and less meaningful than ever. The subprime market for attention will continue to grow until advertising looks less like a market for attention and more like a toll on global commerce. AI will continue to optimize everything that is measurable, while the things most meaningful for people and businesses, such as culture, storytelling, trust and human connection—the hardest things for machines to measure—will be neglected.

But this new era of AI also creates a rare chance for a reset. AI can be built to serve people rather than keep them scrolling; helping us manage our time, filter information, make better decisions, and reclaim our attention. That would free us to spend it on what matters most: the stories we love, the experiences that bring us joy and, ideally, genuine connection with other people. That’s a future worth building.

Excerpted from Human Dot AI: How the Fight For Your Attention Became the World’s Biggest Business, by Joe Marchese and Jonathan Bing

In addition to the new app icon, Google Messages for Android is testing a big homepage redesign that has three core components.

Update 11/7: Instead of pinned chats just appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is trying a redesign that significantly elevates them above all conversations.

This redesign takes advantage of the existing background layer that’s currently just home to the logo/wordmark, search, and account menu.

Hate the idea of just the pinned "bobble head" look. I like being able to view message tidbits. Plus, it's directly copying Apple (enough said). I have to use an iPhone at my job. I hate the pinned bubble conversation look and more importantly it's function.

Otherwise, you’ll see a circular magnifying glass icon and “Start chat” in the pill. The animation that accompanies this change looks nice and feels alive, while boosting one-handed usability.

Google has replaced the Gemini FAB with a button in the top-right corner next to your profile image. This matches the design leveraged by Workspace apps on desktop and mobile.

These updates are currently in the beta channel and not yet widely rolled out to all testers. Some users have all aspects of the redesign, but it appears that Google is rolling out the various components in a piecemeal fashion.

#10410. Top 6 AI Image Generators in 2026: Features, Strengths, and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A designer who once spent an afternoon searching stock libraries can now describe the picture they want and have four versions in under a minute. AI image generators have moved from curiosity to everyday tool for blog headers, product mockups, ad concepts, game art and slide decks. The quality gap between tools has narrowed, but the differences that remain matter a lot: how well each follows a detailed prompt, whether it can render readable text, how it handles edits, and what you are allowed to do with the result.

This guide compares six of the best-known options, what each does well and where each falls short. Models, plans and limits change often, so check each vendor's own pages before you commit to a workflow.

OpenArt’s AI image generator puts several image models behind one interface. Its generator page lists models including GPT Image 2.5, Grok Imagine, Qwen Image 3, Nano Banana 2 and Seedream 5.0 Pro, and lets you create images from text prompts or reference photos. It also lists tools for camera angle control, upscaling, collages and a Character Builder for keeping characters consistent across scenes, with 4K export.

Best for: Creators who want to compare several models on the same prompt without juggling separate subscriptions and accounts.

Limitations: The page offers a free start but does not state credit amounts or plan details, and it does not address commercial use, so check the pricing and licensing pages before using results for client work. Output quality depends on which model you pick.

OpenAI's image generation in ChatGPT works inside the chat interface, which makes iteration natural: generate an image, then ask for changes in plain language. OpenAI highlights accurate text rendering, the ability to follow prompts with many distinct objects, and consistent characters across multi-turn edits. You can also upload reference images and have the model transform them. It handles both photorealistic and stylized looks.

Best for: Marketers and writers who want to describe, refine and re-describe an image without learning a new tool.

Limitations: OpenAI notes that tall images such as posters can be cropped too tightly, and that dense small text, multilingual text and precise graphs can still go wrong. Images can take up to a minute to render. All generated images carry C2PA metadata identifying their source.

Gemini's image generation runs on Google's Nano Banana models. Google highlights character consistency, text rendering in many languages, combining several photos, precise editing and 2K resolution. A free tier covers image generation and editing, while the most advanced model requires a Google AI plan. You start from the "Create images" option in the Gemini app, then prompt or upload a picture to edit.

Best for: People who need to keep the same subject across several images, or who want to edit existing photos quickly.

Limitations: Usage limits apply, and the strongest model is behind a paid plan. Images include an invisible SynthID watermark and a visible AI label, which is good for transparency but may not suit every use.

Midjourney is an independent research lab known for images with a strong, painterly look. Its official site points users to a sign-up flow and to a Discord community and help center for support. Many creators choose it for concept art, mood boards and illustration where style matters more than literal accuracy.

Best for: Artists, art directors and game designers who want rich, stylized results and enjoy exploring variations.

Limitations: I could not confirm current pricing, trial terms or feature details from Midjourney's public pages, so check them yourself before subscribing. The workflow can feel less like a normal app than the others on this list, and it is not the easiest route for precise, text-heavy graphics.

Adobe Firefly is built for professionals who already work in Creative Cloud. Adobe states that its Firefly models are commercially safe, trained on licensed Adobe Stock and public domain content, and outputs carry Content Credentials that show AI involvement. It offers text-to-image, image-to-image, sketch-to-image and style transfer, plus editing tools such as background removal, object removal, upscaling and generative expand. It connects with Photoshop, Illustrator, Lightroom and Adobe Express, and also lets you use partner models from other companies.

Best for: Designers and brand teams who need clear licensing and want AI inside the apps they already use.

Limitations: Plans work on a credit system, so heavy use adds up. Adobe lists a free tier with limited daily generations and paid plans starting at about $9.99 a month, but confirm current terms on its site.

Ideogram built its reputation on a problem that trips up many generators: readable text. Its current models are presented as producing clean typography in different layouts, with attention to prompt fidelity and reliable editing. It also offers an API with access to a catalog of models, and has released open weights for one earlier model for local use and customization under its license.

Best for: Posters, social graphics, logo concepts and anything where words are part of the image.

Limitations: The pages I checked did not describe a free plan, so look at current plans before relying on it. Like every generator, it still needs a human to proofread the text it produces.

Start with the job. If you want to compare several models side by side, try OpenArt. If you want to talk your way to a finished image, try ChatGPT or Gemini. If you need images that will sit inside a branded design workflow, Firefly is the safer fit. If you are chasing a distinctive look, Midjourney deserves a trial. If text must be perfect, test Ideogram.

Run the same prompt in two or three tools before paying. Differences in composition, hands, faces and text show up quickly, and they matter more than any feature list.

Reviews only go so far, because your own use case is what counts. Pick one realistic job, for example a 16:9 header image for a blog post about web performance, and run the same prompt through two or three tools. Write the prompt once and paste it unchanged, so the comparison is fair:

Then score each result on five questions: Did it follow every instruction? Are there odd details in hands, edges or objects? Is any text spelled correctly? Does it still look good when cropped to a square? Could you license it for your project? Ten minutes of this teaches more than any feature list, and it shows how much editing each tool needs before you can publish.

Most readers of this guide will put these images on web pages, where a few habits matter more than the generator you choose.

There is no single best AI image generator. The right pick depends on whether you value conversation, style, licensing, control or typography. Test two or three on a real project, compare the output, and keep a human in charge of the final choice. Whatever you generate, review it for errors and label AI-made images clearly where your audience would expect it.

Are AI-generated images free to use commercially? It depends on the provider and your plan. Read the licensing terms for the tool you use, and consider vendors that publish how their models were trained if you work for clients.

Which AI image generator is best for text in images? Ideogram and ChatGPT both highlight text rendering, and Gemini lists it as a feature. Test each with your own wording and proofread the result.

Do AI images have watermarks? Some do. OpenAI adds C2PA metadata, Google adds an invisible SynthID watermark and a visible label, and Adobe attaches Content Credentials.

Can I use more than one image model without separate accounts? Yes. Platforms such as OpenArt put several models in one interface, which makes side-by-side testing easier. Check the licensing terms for each model you use.

Should I add alt text to AI-generated images? Yes, when the image carries meaning. Describe what it shows or why it is there. Purely decorative images can use an empty alt attribute, following the W3C guidance.

#10408. Android tablets are back, but are they for you?

Android tablets have always been a bit of a touchy subject, but it’s abundantly clear that the form factor is making a comeback. But, as someone who’s a fan of the smaller sizes, are you actually using the gargantuan Android tablets that every company seems obsessed with? In other words – are you the customer for the Android tablets these brands are selling?

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

For a while there, Android tablets had hit what felt like a dead end. Bigger smartphones and cooling of the tablet market as a whole, along with the general sentiment that Apple was doing a way better job with the iPad anyway, left the category in a place that felt stagnant – and that’s the nice way of putting it.

But, over the past few years, Android tablets have had a renaissance.

New form factors, big releases from a variety of brands, and flagship-tier devices left and right. Despite Android’s push into foldables and still-huge displays on nearly every smartphone, tablets are very much back. Prior to RAMageddon’s worst impacts, tablet sales were growing for nearly everyone, and Android brands were seeing a larger slice of the pie.

Anyway, this is on my mind right now because I’ve had a lot of Android tablets arrive in my office in the past few weeks, capping off a lot of tablet announcements in the past few months. I just finished up with Redmagic Astra 2, a tablet I think fits the description of “Android’s iPad Mini OLED,” and I’m in the process of moving into tablets from Lenovo and Amazon. Our Jordan Floyd has also been testing out the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra behind the scenes. And if there’s one trend amongst recent tablet releases, it’s that big tablets seem to be the primary focus among a lot of brands.

Take Amazon’s new Google Play-equipped Alexa Tablet lineup, for example.

The Alexa Tablet 12 is the crown jewel of the lineup, packing the most powerful specs and a premium anti-glare display. It’s the only one that gets a “Pro” moniker, while the 11-inch and 8-inch models are noticeable steps down. Unboxing the Alexa Tablet 8 this week, for example, I was immediately reminded this is not a premium device – the screen makes that clear without any hesitation whatsoever. It was a case of whiplash after setting up the Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 with its 4K display.

It’s a weird one for me. I’ve never been a big fan of these super-sized Android tablets (or iPads, for that matter). I can get behind a 10-inch or 11-inch model, but I find myself more at home on the smaller slates. They’re fantastic for travel as an alternative to draining my phone’s battery, while I find myself just reaching for a laptop instead if I want a bigger screen. A big tablet, regardless of specs, can rarely replace a proper laptop for me, so lugging both around just sounds like more trouble than it’s worth.

But, clearly, people are buying these bigger slates. Samsung appears to be seeing enough success with its mammoth Galaxy Tab S Ultra lineup to keep the 14.6-inch tablet around each year while the smaller sizes are now on an every-other-year cycle. Lenovo’s lineup is virtually all underpowered when the screen size goes down, aside from the Legion Tab that’s now $900.

Are you buying these bigger tablets? What are you using them for?

I imagine that most folks opting for a bigger tablet are using these in the place of a laptop. Thinner and lighter, longer battery life, etc. And in cases like the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro and its $550~ price tag, I get the appeal. Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 takes that down a notch for me at $799 – you’re getting into laptop territory there – but it still is a compelling-enough alternative if it fits your needs. The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra at $1,400 plus a $200 keyboard, yeah I don’t get that one at all.

Let’s discuss! I want to know if you’re using an Android tablet, what you’re using it for, and what size you actually prefer.

Ladies and gents, we’ve finally got a new flagship in the US. Motorola Signature 27 is launching on November 19 and looks excellent, though its flashy spec sheet won’t come cheap at $1,599.

Finally, something good came out of Googlebook

Googlebook is a disaster, but there’s finally one good thing coming out of it in Henry Cavill’s new “Mustache Protocol” game which, supposedly, was built on Googlebook. I’ll bite my tongue there, but the accompanying video brought a needed bit of joy into my week.

I use an 8" Samsung. Not the best in specs, but fine for browsing and reading books. I had a Nexus 10 years ago and gave it to my sister-in-law as I rarely needed something that big. My wife also uses an 8" Samsung, mostly for reading.

#10406. How To Build Financial AI Capacity As A Competitive Advantage

Dr. Ravi Gedela, CEO, Banking Labs Inc., an AI-powered financial intelligence company.

The global financial system stands at the threshold of a fundamental structural realignment driven by artificial intelligence (AI). It is a paradigm shift at its macro scale, intensified by the fast-paced penetration into vertical domains of global finance and, notably, capital markets, regulatory compliance and financial crime risk management.​

For leaders across large banks, institutional investment firms and payment service providers, navigating this shift is no longer a discretionary IT modernization effort. It is an existential imperative for long-term business growth and market leadership.

However, critical questions remain: Is AI a hyperscale trap of cash flow or a real business growth opportunity? Why do many AI programs stall in large institutions? And what must change for them to succeed?

Over the next decade, financial institutions will experience a dramatic reallocation of enterprise value. Historically, much of a firm’s value has resided in human capital: the knowledge, execution capability and client networks of senior bankers and deal teams. In the emerging operational model, that value anchor migrates to proprietary software architectures, governed data assets and institutional context layers that the firm owns.

Achieving this transition requires leadership to systematically extract the latent domain expertise, tactical judgment and deal-making frameworks locked within the minds of their top human performers and permanently embed them into software assets. By transforming ephemeral human capability into compounding firm-wide intelligence infrastructure, institutions can ensure that their competitive moat expands continuously rather than walking out the door at the close of every business day.

​A common reason AI programs stall is that they often rely exclusively on generalist frontier model providers to run complex financial operations. Frontier labs produce exceptional raw cognitive engines, but they often optimize for horizontal, mass-market scale. Treasury, capital markets and financial crime risk management, by contrast, are specialized, confidential domains governed by strict regulatory mandates, distinct data topologies and exacting precision standards.

Generalist providers are unlikely to build the last-mile intelligence pipelines that finance requires: transaction venues that comply with jurisdiction-specific rules, material non-public information (MNPI) isolation barriers and deep integrations with systems of record, such as Bloomberg or Salesforce. That work would distract from hyperscale revenue targets and add regulatory exposure.

Sustainable value, therefore, requires purpose-built financial AI: architectures that wrap foundation models in operational harnesses, compliance guardrails and domain-specific integration layers. At Banking Labs, where my team builds financial AI across capital markets, compliance and financial crime, we have consistently found that this harness, not the model itself, is where durable advantage is won.

In private markets—where workflows historically suffered from manual human coordination, fragmented data and non-standardized documentation—vertical AI architectures can systematically execute core operational processes:

1. Data Room Preparation And Tearing: Agents can autonomously ingest, organize, cross-examine and extract key metrics from incoming virtual data room documents, cross-referencing company performance against firm-specific investment mandates.

2. Confidential Information Memorandum (CIM) Drafting: The system can synthesize internal financial models, market positioning data and competitive landscapes into comprehensive, publication-ready deal decks and investment committee memos.

3. Buyer Outreach And DDQ Processing: AI can facilitate the autonomous coordination of targeted buyer lists, tailored outreach tracking and the automated intake, resolution and verification of complex due diligence questionnaires (DDQs).

4. Executive Markup Workflows: These systems can help modernize senior leadership interfaces by enabling executives to mark up presentations directly on mobile devices or via email. The AI harness can parse these handwritten or text markups, execute structural edits across underlying files and return fully revised presentation decks within, in my experience, 20 minutes (down from a standard two-day turnaround using junior staff). Simultaneously, the engine can generate complete, transparent audit trails detailing every modification for junior bankers to inspect and verify.

While private markets require the constant navigation of unstructured data, public markets can present structured, data-rich environments ideal for advanced multiagent architectures. In these venues, firms can deploy sophisticated agentic frameworks, such as multiagent debate clusters. While automated execution can dramatically accelerate transaction velocity, operating at scale requires rigorous compliance architectures to ensure speed never compromises legal defensibility.​

Model risk management is being reshaped in both the United States and Canada. In April 2026, U.S. banking regulators replaced SR 11-7, the guidance that had governed model risk for 15 years, with SR 26-2. The new framework is more principles-based, and regulators have indicated that AI-specific expectations will follow.

Canada is moving in the same direction. OSFI’s revised Guideline E-23, effective May 1, 2027, brings AI and machine learning models explicitly within its scope. Its approach is proportional: Models with greater autonomy or customer impact require closer review and monitoring.

Institutions operating in both countries must therefore satisfy two regimes on different timelines. Both, however, require AI that is governed, explainable and auditable. General-purpose models struggle to meet this standard on their own. Vertical financial AI, designed with lineage and controls from the outset, is better positioned to do so.

In institutional compliance, lineage auditability outranks raw statistical accuracy. A highly accurate model that operates as a black box cannot withstand a regulatory examination or judicial discovery. In the agentic era, explaining a single model is not enough; institutions must be able to prove, step-by-step, how every AI-assisted decision was made.

This answers the questions I began with. AI can become a cash trap when institutions treat it as a technology function delegated to large vendors offering frontier models. It becomes a growth engine when they invest in domain-specific, vertical AI capacity that they own and govern. Large institutions should pivot from the convenience of outsourcing AI to the discipline of building AI capital.

Before the next budget cycle, executives should ask one question: If a regulator asked tomorrow why our AI made a specific decision, could we show them, step-by-step, how it came to that decision?​​

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Valve is adding framerate telemetry data to games so you can see what your hardware will manage in a given game before you buy it. The new initiative will start with the Steam Deck, but Valve has promised to bring the feature to more hardware in the future, presumably not only its Steam Machine but desktop gaming PCs more generally. The new feature shows players' average FPS on Steam Deck while playing the title, so customers can decide whether to invest without risking a purchase.

Valve already added the option to insert your hardware specifications when you write a review for a game, but an extremely small fraction of players actually write reviews, and from looking at reviews on recent Steam games, it seems like an even smaller fraction actually select to include their hardware specifications, for whatever reason.

The clever among you may have realized "but wait, PC games have settings you can adjust, so even the same hardware might deliver really different performance levels." Correct! And it's also exactly why Valve is doing this. Its Steam Deck Verified program requires a certain level of performance, and games can get marked as "Unsupported" if they don't reach that level, but some people may find them playable regardless. In other words, there's no one perfect standard for "playable performance," and thus Valve wants to let users decide for themselves.

Valve says that, at least for this early trial with Steam Deck data, that data is being filtered to only show data from Decks that are set to the default frame limit. The firm doesn't make any attempt to account for custom in-game settings, yet it says that "despite this, [Valve has] found that the framerate data consolidates around relatively narrow ranges," after accounting for the unusual effects of vertical sync.

So what if you don't have a Steam Deck? Well, Valve says it sees this update (adding the Steam Deck framerate data) as "a stepping stone toward providing framerate data for more devices than just Steam Deck." Obviously, that includes Valve's own Steam Machine mini-desktop and Steam Frame VR headset, but presumably it will extend to folks on standard gaming PCs (whether desktop or laptop)

It's not clear whether desktop performance data will be matched by graphics card, some combination of GPU and CPU, or multiple factors, but either way, there's no question that this is yet another feature that sets Steam as a storefront above its competitors. If you'd like to opt in, you'll have to join the Steam Client Beta for now; Valve says the feature is coming to all users "in the future," though.

#10399. Which MCM Has the Best Revshare? A Developer’s Guide to Evaluating Ad Partners

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An ad partner’s revenue share looks easy to compare: keeping 90% sounds better than keeping 80%. But the percentage does not tell a developer what will happen when the integration reaches production. Extra JavaScript, unstable ad slots, opaque reporting, and difficult rollbacks can change the value of an apparently attractive deal.

For teams maintaining an advertising-funded website, choosing a Multiple Customer Management (MCM) partner is partly an engineering decision. The integration affects page templates, consent handling, third-party requests, account access, and monitoring. Those changes deserve the same scrutiny as a new analytics SDK or payment integration.

This guide explains how to compare revenue shares on a consistent basis, review integration requirements, and test an ad setup without sacrificing usability. The goal is a repeatable evaluation process, rather than a universal winner.

Google Ad Manager’s MCM system lets a parent publisher manage a child publisher’s account or delegated inventory. The commercial agreement defines the partner’s services and compensation. Before comparing offers, ask which revenue streams the quoted percentage covers and whether the reporting figure is before or after that fee.

Use three separate lines in your evaluation spreadsheet:

Revenue base: record the amount to which the partner’s percentage applies. Advertiser spending, exchange-reported revenue, and publisher earnings are different figures. Do not treat them as interchangeable.

Partner compensation: identify the percentage, fixed charges, and any optional services. Ask whether the same terms apply to every demand source and ad format.

Adjustments: distinguish estimated revenue from finalized earnings, including invalid-traffic deductions and other corrections. Document when adjustments appear and which party bears them.

A common mistake is applying the partner fee twice because a dashboard already displays net revenue. Label each exported metric before using it in a comparison.

The two delegation models have different implications for access, reporting, and payments. Google’s documentation is the starting point for checking the proposed setup.

Manage Account gives the parent edit access within the child’s account while the child retains access and permissions. Payment facilitation can allocate eligible earnings from the child’s primary Ad Exchange account, but it does not automatically cover every third-party revenue stream. Confirm the invitation’s payment percentage and the separate commercial agreement.

Manage Inventory lets the parent manage delegated inventory in its own account, without access to the child account. Reporting for that inventory sits in the parent account. Google pays the parent for the relevant inventory, and the parent pays the child according to their agreement. Ask how you will obtain reports and reconcile payments.

Before implementation, document who can change tags, ad units, consent settings, and demand configuration. Agree on access for debugging and exporting historical data. A developer should be able to trace a production request to its configuration owner.

Use this table as a request-for-information checklist. It does not rank providers or assert that any named service supports a particular implementation. Obtain current terms and technical documentation for the product you are considering.

Apply the same standards to every proposal. The following examples show what a developer should ask during evaluation; each question is relevant across providers.

MonetizeMore offers publisher monetization products, including PubGuru and Traffic Cop. When evaluating its proposal, connect the commercial discussion to concrete integration questions: which scripts will load, who owns the configuration, and how will reported earnings be reconciled?

Request a sample report showing the revenue base, partner fee, and deductions as separate fields. Check whether the proposed plan includes every service shown in the sales demonstration.

Ask for a written ownership map covering Ad Manager access, tag deployment, configuration changes, and incident response. Identify who can restore the previous setup if delivery fails.

During a trial, compare representative templates and devices. Record script requests and main-thread activity alongside net revenue, using the same measurement definitions for the existing setup.

Decision criterion: choose on measured results and documented responsibilities, rather than assuming that a quoted split predicts final earnings.

For any proposal involving a header-bidding wrapper, including one from Setupad, ask how the wrapper fits into your existing page lifecycle.

Review bidder configuration, auction timeouts, and when the ad server receives targeting information. A missing bid and an unfilled ad slot are different problems.

Check whether your team can inspect the active configuration and reproduce an issue on a test page. Agree on who approves changes to bidders or timeout values.

Measure the complete sequence: consent readiness, auction start, bid responses, ad request, and rendering. Avoid attributing every delay to the same component.

Decision criterion: the implementation should be observable enough to explain failures, with commercial terms verified separately.

When assessing Publisher Collective or another managed partner, establish how the proposed setup could be tested on a limited, agreed scope.

Ask whether rollout can be restricted to selected templates or an eligible traffic cohort. Do not assume partial testing is available until the partner confirms it.

Record device, geography, page type, and consent state so differences in traffic mix do not masquerade as a revenue improvement.

Keep a dated deployment log connecting each configuration version with the reporting period.

Decision criterion: a measured comparison should separate implementation changes from changes in audience or demand.

A proposal from AdPushup or another optimization provider may involve changes to ad placement. Review the actual proposed changes with both design and engineering.

Check spacing, responsive behavior, keyboard navigation, and whether sticky placements obscure content or controls.

Reserve space for expected ad dimensions and test what happens when no ad is returned.

Compare layout stability before and after the change.

Decision criterion: additional earnings should be assessed alongside usability and performance, with explicit acceptance criteria.

For an Ezoic proposal, as for any managed platform, start with the exact integration method offered to your site.

List required changes to scripts, plugins, caching, DNS, or delivery infrastructure, if any. Do not assume that every deployment uses the same method.

Test interactions with your consent manager, content security policy, caching rules, and existing analytics.

Document how to remove the integration and restore the prior configuration.

Decision criterion: the operational cost should be visible before the first production rollout.

When reviewing a Monumetric proposal, establish which implementation work belongs to your team and which belongs to the provider.

Ask who creates ad slots, updates templates, and validates responsive sizes.

Request a support escalation process with the diagnostic information required for an incident: URL, timestamp, device, consent state, and affected slot.

Confirm onboarding costs and payment terms in writing.

Decision criterion: routine changes and production failures should have a clear owner.

Chrome DevTools helps trace third-party requests in the Network panel and investigate long tasks in the Performance panel. Capture a baseline before deployment, then repeat the same navigation and interaction sequence after deployment. Use comparable device and network settings.

Google Publisher Console helps investigate Google Publisher Tag ad slots and delivery issues. For a Prebid-based setup, use Prebid’s debugging tools to inspect the auction path. These tools answer different questions: whether the auction behaved as expected and whether the ad server delivered the requested slot.

PageSpeed Insights provides performance diagnostics; distinguish its lab results from available field data. Add web-vitals to your own monitoring when you need measurements associated with a deployment or cohort. Track LCP, INP, and CLS alongside revenue instead of treating a single Lighthouse score as the complete user experience.

Reserve responsive space for ad slots before content arrives, and investigate shifts when empty slots collapse. SitePoint’s guide to web performance optimization explains related techniques for loading JavaScript, reducing layout work, and managing long tasks.

With the same traffic volume, revenue definition, and deduction rate, the break-even increase in pre-partner revenue is: (current publisher share ÷ new publisher share) − 1. Express shares consistently as fractions or percentages. The table below shows the required lift; it is not a forecast these thresholds only describe the arithmetic. Different ad density, audience mix, deduction rates, or reporting bases can invalidate the comparison. Normalize to the same denominator, such as revenue per thousand pageviews, and compare matched periods or properly assigned concurrent cohorts.

Assume two hypothetical setups each receive one million pageviews. Here, RPM means revenue per thousand pageviews before the partner fee. For this simplified example, deductions reduce that revenue before the publisher share is applied.

Partner A: $10 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.90 after deductions × 0.90 publisher share = $8,100 net revenue.

Partner B: $12 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.98 after deductions × 0.80 publisher share = $9,408 net revenue.

The difference is $1,308 for the period despite Partner B’s lower share. These are illustrative inputs, not provider performance claims. Faster payment improves cash-flow timing; it does not, by itself, increase the revenue earned.

Use Playwright with mocked responses or test creatives in a controlled environment to check slow loading, empty slots, blocked scripts, and navigation between routes. Verify that the page remains usable when the ad system fails. Automated tests should not click live advertisements or generate artificial monetized traffic.

Separate unit tests for configuration logic, integration tests for component boundaries, and browser tests for user-visible behavior. SitePoint’s explanation of unit, functional, and integration testing provides a useful foundation. Define rollback criteria before launch, keep the control configuration available, and review finalized revenue alongside performance data before expanding the deployment.

There is no universal answer from the percentage alone. Compare current written offers using the same revenue base, then evaluate finalized net earnings, performance, access, and implementation effort.

Not necessarily. Reports may differ in timezone, currency, transaction coverage, fee treatment, and finalization date. Reconcile those definitions before treating a discrepancy as an integration bug.

Ask how renewals, volume tiers, optional services, and rate changes are handled. Record the applicable terms with the configuration and reporting period used for your evaluation.

No. If deductions and the revenue base are otherwise comparable, an 80% share needs 12.5% more pre-partner revenue to match a 90% share. Measure whether that lift exists rather than assuming it.

Do not treat any protection claim as a guarantee. Ask how suspected invalid traffic is handled, what evidence is available, and how later adjustments are reflected in your reports and payments.

Choose the setup that produces verifiable net value while meeting the site’s performance and operational requirements. A good evaluation leaves your team with reproducible measurements, understandable reports, and a practical rollback plan—not just a favorable percentage.
