#10397. The Illusion Of The Industry Standard: Cyber Resilience Across Sectors

Sivan Tehila is the CEO and Founder of Onyxia Cyber and Cybersecurity Masters Program Director at the YU Katz School of Science and Health.

​For years, “industry standard” has done a great deal of quiet work in cybersecurity. In boardrooms and vendor briefings alike, it has become shorthand for “safe enough,” a way to settle a hard question by pointing to what everyone else appears to be doing. But when we surveyed 300 CISOs across financial services, healthcare and pharma, critical infrastructure, IT and technology, and retail and e-commerce for our latest research report, the data told a different story. There is no single bar. What one sector treats as an unacceptable exposure, another absorbs as the cost of doing business, and most security leaders have little visibility into where they actually sit within that range.​

Consider one of the most fundamental tasks in security: patching a critical vulnerability. In IT and technology, 69% of leaders prioritize closing that window within three days. In critical infrastructure, the sector behind our power, water and transportation systems, only 31% do. The threat is identical, and the clock is the same, yet fewer than half keep pace.​

This is not an outlier. It is the pattern that runs through nearly every metric we measured. Not a single CISO in healthcare or critical infrastructure reports that their sector demands 100% MFA coverage—compared to 35% in financial services who do. The average acceptable phishing simulation reporting rate stands at over 78% in IT and technology but falls to 59.9% in critical infrastructure.

Yet even the strongest performers carry hidden costs: Financial services sets the pace on speed and hygiene, yet posts the worst security-operations signal-to-noise of any sector, with false-positive rates above 13% that bury its analysts in alerts. There is no single industry standard. There are industry divides.​

These divides matter more than they used to because attackers do not organize themselves by industry. The same commodity techniques, such as credential stuffing against accounts without MFA, lateral movement through unmanaged devices or a single unpatched flaw, translate across every vertical.

When an entire sector agrees that a given level of exposure is acceptable, it is, in effect, agreeing on where the easiest entry points will be. And as the attack surface undergoes a massive, AI-driven expansion, that agreement grows more dangerous: Automated reconnaissance and exploit tooling let adversaries find the slowest sector and the open window faster, and at lower cost, than ever before. Because our infrastructure is interconnected through shared vendors and supply chains, one industry’s definition of “acceptable” rarely stays contained to that industry.​

The deeper problem is that most of these numbers are invisible to the people living inside them. “Acceptable risk” is rarely a decision anyone set out to make. More often, it is an inherited default, the level of exposure that came to feel normal because the organizations nearby appeared to tolerate it. No one formally signed off on running 4% noncompliant devices; the number simply accumulated. That is what makes these benchmarks so consequential. It is hard to defend a threshold no one ever consciously chose.​

So what should security leaders do? Three things, in order.

“Industry standard” is only useful once you know which industry you are measuring against and whether its norms hold up next to a tougher bar elsewhere. Frequently, they do not.

A healthcare CISO who matches the healthcare average of 4.41% noncompliant devices is matching a number more than 50% higher than the 2.91% financial services holds itself to, on the exact same control. That gap needs to be explained at the business level, not inherited silently.​

If an organization tolerates a percentage of accounts without multifactor authentication, or a degree of patch-SLA slippage, that figure should be one a leader chose deliberately and can defend, not a gap discovered after an incident. Naming the number is what converts a blind spot into a managed risk.​

Resilience is not a snapshot assembled for an audit; it is a posture an organization holds under pressure. These divides persist in large part because too many teams see their own position only periodically, in fragments, well after the data has gone stale. It is difficult to challenge an inherited standard that you can only glimpse once a quarter. The leaders who close the gap will be those who replace occasional self-assessment with continuous, quantified and increasingly AI-driven insight into where they stand, the kind that surfaces a weakening control before an adversary does.​

The most important finding in this year’s research is not any single statistic. It is that the reassurance of “industry standard” is largely an illusion, and an increasingly costly one. Having spent years as a CISO, I understand its appeal; a benchmark makes a hard call feel settled. But our responsibility was never to match the room.

By benchmarking against real risk, naming the exposure you are willing to accept and measuring it without interruption, you stop inheriting a standard and start setting one. This turns visibility into actionability and the kind of operational cyber resilience your organization actually depends on. The sooner we raise that bar together, across every sector, the harder we make the adversary’s work and the better we do our own.​

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Prusa has patched all the vulnerabilities discovered ahead of a coordinated news release.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Software engineer Yannick Dixken spent a week attacking his Prusa MK4S 3D printer in the name of science. At the end of the relatively short but intense period, he produced a video demonstrating the ability to Rickroll the printer via remote code execution (RCE). Dixken shared the video and findings – charting “roughly 23 individual defects” with Prusa and published his amusing but detailed Never gonna print you up! blog in coordination with the 3D printer maker. Yes, all the vulnerabilities are now patched in the Buddy firmware versions >7.0.0.

Dixken is an experienced Freelance Cloud Architect, DevOps and Platform Engineer. Security research is more of a hobby, he notes in the blog post, but it is clearly a passion strong enough to spend a whole week probing the MK4S for vulnerabilities. The result is far more than the funny old Rickroll. The week of debugging, fuzzing and reverse engineering “armed with Opus 4.8 and a fuzzer” resulted in “14 findings, roughly 23 individual defects, and a chain that ends with the printer's main controller running code I sent it over the network,” noted Dixken. “Yup, fully fledged RCE.”

The headlining RCE scored 8.1 and is officially described as High Severity. This serious bug was in the cloud (or self-hosted) management platform called Prusa Connect. You can see proof-of-concept code Rickrolling the user in Dixken’s embedded video. He sent this video to Prusa.

The methods used to uncover these vulnerabilities are outlined in the source blog, if you’d like to know more. Meanwhile, there were many other vulnerabilities uncovered and cataloged. These include a USB filename attack, heap overflows triggered by malformed encrypted print files, and network denial-of-service flaws. Many of the bugs were probably symptoms of the original developers’ use of assert statements to enforce assumptions.

Happily for Prusa 3D printer users, Dixken has responsibly disclosed this multitude of vulnerabilities. The engineer says that within 24 hours of the Rickroll video being shared on social media, the 3D printing firm’s team coordinated professionally, efficiently, and kindly. Companies don’t always react so positively to those helping them find vulnerabilities in their wares.

VR leaker Nori posted a screenshot on X showing a handful of 3D movies coming to the Meta VR Plus service. Considering there is no such Meta VR Plus service currently, the obvious conclusion is that Meta Horizon+ is being renamed once again.

Meta Horizon+ currently includes over 100 games with its $7.99 per month subscription and is similar to Microsoft’s Xbox Game Pass service in many ways. Unironically, Meta Horizon+ also includes the basic Xbox Game Pass tier with over 50 Xbox games playable via the Game Pass cloud. Meta offers a 3-month trial with every new Meta Quest purchase.

The new Meta VR+ service is purported to include 3D movies as well, although we don’t yet know if this will be included in the regular $7.99 per month rate, or if Meta will be introducing additional content tiers, as services like Netflix, Disney+, Xbox Game Pass, and others do. Based on the screenshot, these will be big-name movies and are likely positioned to enhance the value of the upcoming $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, although all the same content will work on existing Meta Quest 3 units.

Meta has been slowly distancing itself from the “Horizon” name ever since the beginning of this year, when its VR division got a big reset. In a February blog post, Samantha Ryan, the VP of Content at Meta’s Reality Labs, spoke about the changes to the company’s strategy, including the loss of most in-house VR gaming studios. Since then, several prominent VR developers from Meta have gone on to create independent studios, including the super-popular Supernatural exercise app.

Meta then decoupled the unpopular Horizon Metaverse from its headsets, moving it to mobile-only, and has been removing the “Horizon” name from just about everything since then. Meta Horizon+ looks to be the latest big change, as the company moves toward “Meta VR” branding, which is clearer and separates its VR division from mobile and smart glasses efforts.

Rebooted by Hileeq has shared how others can get cheap Lenovo ThinkPads and save them from becoming e-waste by using a simple BIOS unlock hack that only requires a $10 programmer and another laptop or PC. The technique is niche, known mostly by technicians, but Hileeq is the first to give this bypass mass attention with an easy-to-follow YouTube tutorial.

Rebooted by Hileeq's channel, dedicated to fixing cheap eBay finds, documents the process and what he learned while fixing the laptops. Three weeks ago, he posted a video explaining how to bypass locked Lenovo ThinkPads with Intel 4th- to 8th-generation CPUs using a cheap CH431A programmer to read, write, erase, and save EEPROM and SPI flash memory.

Companies often add supervisor passwords to the fleet of ThinkPads they hand out to their employees as an IT security measure. When these ThinkPads are disposed of, often with the storage removed and destroyed, it’s rare that the supervisor passwords are included and documented. These locked ThinkPads are then incredibly cheap because of the lack of access, ending up as e-waste most of the time. However, Victor Voinea shared a post in a Romanian forum containing his ThinkPad supervisor removal exploits.

Unfortunately, Voinea’s method generated a random password every time the exploit was run, requiring users to contact Voinea for the key specific to the generated hardware ID — and getting the password wasn’t free. However, in 2020, Knucklegrumble posted a free way to bypass the password in the Badcaps electronics repair forum. Mark Juvan, an Ethical Hacker, reverse-engineered Knucklegrumble’s exploit as his cybersecurity master’s thesis at Radboud University Nijmegen, Netherlands, which goes into deeper detail.

The exploit begins by extracting the BIOS from the EEPROM chip on the motherboard using the CH341A programmer and plugging it into a USB port of another PC or laptop. Hileeq then uses NeoProgrammer, a utility for CH341A programmers, and dumps the BIOS, saving a copy of it on the other laptop. NeoProgrammer then applies the same auto-patching workflow Knucklegrumble created.

When the patched BIOS is flashed onto the EEPROM, the laptop can then be turned on, and Hileeq goes through some steps requiring a few keystrokes which remove the password saved in the Embedded Controller (EC), a separate IC that stores security data, among other system tasks. The original BIOS can then be flashed back into the EEPROM, and with the supervisor password removed, the laptop is now usable.

Juvan states in his paper that the exploit takes advantage of a weakness in Lenovo’s firmware verification and driver architecture. Lenovo actually provides the EmulatedEepromDxe driver needed by the exploit, and the driver allows the EEPROM to be read and written to — and the EC’s supervisor password happens to be stored where it’s treated as EEPROM memory, allowing the supervisor password to be overwritten or removed.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The hard, complicated work has already been done by the electronics repair community, and now the process to bypass the supervisor password requires just a few steps and an inexpensive programmer tool. While the method may only be for ThinkPads with Intel 4th- to 8th-generation CPUs, this will still save plenty of usable ThinkPads from going to waste, as Hileeq’s popular post potentially encourages more people to attempt this themselves — who knows, this might cause a domino effect to unlock newer generations of ThinkPads.

#10386. Top 6 AI Video Generators in 2026: Features, Strengths, and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A year ago, most AI video clips lasted a few seconds, had no sound and drifted off-model by the final frame. Today several tools produce 1080p or even 4K clips with synchronized audio, camera control and reference-based consistency. The market also moves quickly: OpenAI announced it was shutting down Sora in March 2026, so the list of tools worth using has changed.

This guide compares six AI video generators that developers, designers and marketers can use today. For each one you will see what it does well, where it falls short and who it suits. Plans, credits and model names change often, so confirm details on each vendor’s site before you commit.

OpenArt’s AI video generator puts a range of video models behind one interface. Its page lists models such as Veo 3.1, Kling, Seedance, Wan, Hailuo and PixVerse, so you can run the same prompt on different engines and compare the results without managing separate accounts.

Beyond text-to-video and image-to-video, it offers start and end frame control, video-to-video restyling, motion transfer from a reference clip, a character builder for consistency, lip sync and conversational editing for tasks such as swapping a background or relighting a scene. Resolution goes up to 4K on many models, with 1080p as the default, and clips are usually up to 15 seconds, with longer limits on a few models.

Strengths: model variety, a single credit pool, editing tools alongside generation and a shared library for your clips.

Limits: credit use varies by model, so it is worth testing short clips first. Commercial-use rights depend on your plan and on the model you pick, so check the pricing and terms pages.

Best for: creators and small teams that want to compare models quickly instead of committing to one.

Veo is Google DeepMind’s video model. Veo 3.1 generates sound effects, ambient noise and dialogue together with the video, supports image-to-video, first and last frame transitions, reference images for characters or objects, and outputs 1080p and 4K. You can reach it through the Gemini app, Google Flow and the Gemini API.

Strengths: audio generated with the picture, strong prompt adherence and an API that fits into developer workflows.

Limits: base clips are short, around 8 seconds, so longer scenes rely on scene extension. Dialogue quality in short segments is still being refined, and access and quotas depend on your Google plan.

Best for: developers and marketers who want audio and video from one prompt, or who plan to automate generation through an API.

Runway has been a staple of AI filmmaking since its early Gen models. Its pricing page lists Gen-4.5 and Aleph alongside partner models, and the paid plans include all video and image models, 4K upscaling and parallel generations. Higher tiers add features such as voice clones, brand kits and HDR or ProRes output.

Strengths: polished editing tools, video-to-video workflows and a professional output pipeline that suits post-production teams.

Limits: credits are consumed quickly on premium models, and on the lower paid plans they do not roll over from month to month.

Best for: video editors and agencies that need control over shots and want AI to fit into an existing editing process.

Kling from Kuaishou has built a reputation for natural motion and expressive characters. The current release, Kling 4.0, sits alongside tools such as Motion Control, a canvas workspace, an agent and MCP or CLI batch generation for teams that want to automate production.

Strengths: realistic movement, motion transfer and batch tools for producing many short clips.

Limits: the main site does not spell out all clip-length and resolution limits for each model, so check the model page you plan to use. Pricing and free credits vary by region and plan.

Best for: social video, product shots and character-driven clips where motion quality is the priority.

Luma’s Dream Machine is built on the Ray model family. Its current page lists Ray3.2 and Ray3.14, along with a “Modify video” tool that restyles footage, extends duration and reframes aspect ratios. It also lists camera-motion controls and high-quality EXR export for professional pipelines.

Strengths: reshooting or restyling existing footage, camera-motion control and pipeline-friendly export.

Limits: paid plans start at around $30 per month (or less when billed yearly), and heavy use pushes you into the higher tiers.

Best for: filmmakers and designers who want to modify and extend footage rather than only generate new clips.

Adobe Firefly offers text-to-video and image-to-video with Adobe’s own Firefly Video Model. It also provides partner models, including Google Veo 3.1, Luma Ray3, Kling and Runway Gen-4.5, so you can compare outputs from inside one product. An Assembler and AI video editor let you trim, reorder, extend and add voiceovers, music and sound effects.

Adobe states that the Firefly Video Model is trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public domain material, and describes its output as safe for commercial use. Partner models may carry different terms, so read the details for whichever model you choose.

Strengths: a clear licensing story for the native model, integration with Adobe’s creative apps and an included editor.

Limits: most clips run up to 8 seconds, with some models reaching 15. Credits are allocated monthly, and premium partner models can use them faster.

Best for: brand and in-house teams that care about provenance and already work in Adobe tools.

The table summarizes what each vendor’s own pages say at the time of writing. “Entry paid plan” figures are US prices billed annually where the vendor offers that option.

Credit counts are hard to compare, so convert them to clips. Runway’s pricing page lists Gen-4.5 at 60 credits per 5-second clip, which means the 625 monthly credits on the Standard plan cover roughly ten clips. Adobe says its Standard plan’s 2,000 credits equal up to 40 five-second videos, and OpenArt’s Starter plan lists about 50 videos for 4,000 credits. Premium models cost more: the same Runway page lists Aleph 2.0 at 140 credits per 5 seconds.

Plan for waste. If you keep one usable clip out of every three attempts, your real cost per finished shot is about three times the sticker price. Test with short, low-resolution drafts, then render the winner at full quality.

Because every tool outputs short clips, the real work is assembly. A typical workflow is: write a shot list, generate two or three takes per shot, pick the best, normalize them to one format, join them and add captions and audio. FFmpeg handles the joining step from the command line:

Matching resolution, frame rate and codec before joining avoids glitches at the cut points. For character consistency across shots, reuse the same reference image in every prompt and keep descriptions of the subject identical.

If the clip ends up on your own site, treat it like any other media. Provide a poster image, load metadata only until the visitor presses play, and include captions so deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and anyone watching without sound, can follow along. The W3C’s guidance on captions and subtitles explains what to include, and the MDN video element reference covers the attributes below.

Also write a text description or transcript near the video. Search engines and screen reader users cannot see the footage, so the surrounding text is what explains it.

Short, structured prompts beat long, vague ones. Describe the elements in the order a director would:

Change one element at a time between takes so you can tell which change improved the result.

Marketing demos show the best of a tool, so run your own test. Use the same prompt, duration and aspect ratio on each tool, generate a few takes and score them against a short checklist. Keep notes on how many credits each usable clip costs.

Run the same test again with an image-to-video input if your workflow starts from product photos or illustrations. That often exposes differences in consistency that text prompts hide.

Which AI video generator is best? There is no single winner. Veo is strong for audio, Runway for editing, Kling for motion, Luma for modifying footage and Firefly for licensing clarity. A multi-model tool such as OpenArt helps you compare them.

Can AI video generators make long videos? Not in one pass. Most models create short clips, so longer videos are built by extending or stitching clips together.

Is Sora still available? OpenAI announced in March 2026 that it was shutting down the Sora app and API, so it is not a safe choice for new projects.

Can I use AI videos commercially? Often, but it depends on the plan and the underlying model. Read the current terms before publishing.

How do I keep a character consistent across clips? Reuse the same reference image, keep the subject description identical in every prompt, and use character or reference tools where the platform offers them.

Should I add captions to AI-generated video? Yes. Captions help accessibility and viewers watching without sound, and they give search engines text to index.

Do I need a powerful computer? No. These services run in the cloud, so a browser and a stable connection are enough.

The best AI video generator depends on what you make. Start with a short test prompt, compare a few tools, and keep the one that gives you usable clips at a sensible credit cost. If you are not sure where to begin, a multi-model option such as OpenArt lets you try several engines before you settle on one.

As more information about the ongoing situation at Nvidia unravels, U.S. President Donald Trump has confirmed that the FBI is investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy days after he admitted to the indiscretion. According to the Associated Press, the president said this during a briefing at the White House, with one reporter asking him about his knowledge of Huang’s issue before it became publicly known. The news comes amidst a separate bombshell report from Bloomberg, which claims that Nvidia intervened in a US government probe of suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was an executive.

“Well, I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading about it over a period of time, but, uh, not too long ago,” Trump said. “We’ll look into, I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something, and I think he’ll be in good shape.” He also said, “I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how you’re doing. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

It has been previously reported that U.S. intelligence services suspected that Alice Huang, who previously held an executive position at Megaspeed, had ties to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS), which is one of the country’s intelligence services, and that they told the President about it over a year ago. However, it was reported he did not act on the information, as he reportedly did not want to jeopardize Nvidia sales or antagonize Beijing, especially after the White House approved the export of H200 chips to China with an attached 25% fee.

Congress has called Huang once to confront him about these rumors, with the CEO confirming his affair with Alice Huang shortly after. The committee said it has "concerns over Nvidia’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and Mr. Huang’s reported ties to a Chinese intelligence-linked executive of a Singapore-based data center company.” Now, it seems that the FBI, which is the U.S.’s primary domestic counterintelligence agency, is looking into the situation, too.

While the infidelity of tech executives is usually outside the purview of politicians and law enforcement, Jensen Huang’s sensitive position as the head of the leading AI chip manufacturer that arguably single-handedly drove the global AI race has made him a prominent target. China has denied the accusation that Alice Huang is its agent, but a think tank suggests that “China is employing ‘attractive women’ posing as investors, business professionals, academics, or romantic partners to gain access to U.S. tech talent, networks, and research infrastructure.”

This is why Nvidia’s supposed intervention in the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security’s (BIS) investigation into Megaspeed is becoming a concern. Megaspeed has been investigated for allegedly smuggling $2 billion worth of Nvidia AI processors into China, although Nvidia has claimed that it has done its due diligence and did not find any signs of diversions by the company. Despite that, Bloomberg reports that Nvidia executive vice president and general counsel Tim Teter reached out to U.S. Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security and BIS head Jeffrey Kessler to ask about the administration’s investigation into the company and whether the BIS was involved in Singapore’s detention of Alice Huang at that time. Sources claimed that the U.S. agency was not involved in Ms. Huang’s apprehension by Singaporean authorities.

The publication reported BIS staff were told to route all Nvidia requests through Kessler or to seek approval from him for any outreach involving the company, which people say was highly unusual, and that Teter even supposedly reached out directly to BIS employees. When the affected employees forwarded the emails to Kessler and raised their concerns, the BIS chief instructed them to handle the case by the book. But in late 2025, the Justice Department, which was working alongside the BIS, asked the bureau to pause its efforts on the Megaspeed investigation.

Even though Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, who was linked to Megaspeed and is suspected to be working at the behest of Beijing, there is still no clear proof that Ms. Huang had a direct role in influencing the Nvidia chief to push for the resumption of Nvidia AI chip sales to China. Still, the unraveling of this supposed spy plot has caught the attention of the American leadership, and they’re now asking questions about Nvidia’s security protocols and the company’s sway on Washington.

#10378. 7 E-commerce UX Tips for Selling Car Accessories and Home & Kitchen Products Online

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Here is a question a product page should answer in about five seconds: “Will this magnetic phone mount hold my phone with the case still on?” When the answer is hard to find, shoppers tend to open another tab instead of contacting support.

Stores that sell both car accessories and home & kitchen products face an extra challenge: two very different catalogs share one site. A car accessories buyer cares about fit, mounting and compatibility. A home & kitchen buyer cares about size, capacity and how easy the product is to clean. A single generic product page frustrates both.

This guide covers seven practical e-commerce UX tips that designers and developers can apply right away, with code snippets and a checklist at the end.

A car mount and a vegetable peeler should not share the same spec table. Keep a single reusable product page component and change only the fields based on category. The layout stays consistent, while each shopper sees the details they need.

In code, this can be a config object that your template reads from:

Showing “Not specified” instead of hiding a missing field is a small habit with a real benefit: it makes gaps in your product data visible to your own team.

Shoppers look for deal-breaker information near the price and the purchase button: fit, size and compatibility. Do not bury it in an “Additional information” tab halfway down the page.

A short comparison table also works better than three paragraphs of marketing copy, because shoppers scan rather than read. Baymard Institute’s product page research consistently finds that unclear or hard-to-find specifications are a common reason shoppers hesitate.

A responsive layout is the starting point, not the finish line. People compare car accessories in a parking lot and browse kitchen gadgets while standing in the kitchen, often with one thumb.

A phone mount on a white background says nothing about how it attaches to a dashboard. Show it in a real car, from the driver’s point of view. For home & kitchen products, place the item next to something familiar, like a coffee mug, so people can judge its size.

Good alt text matters for accessibility and for image search. Compare “phone mount” with “Magnetic phone mount fixed to a car dashboard, holding a phone in landscape mode”. The W3C alt text decision tree is a useful guide for deciding what to describe.

Keep images fast, too. Responsive sources with srcset and sizes, explicit dimensions and lazy loading help prevent layout shift and slow pages:

One caveat: do not lazy-load the main product image at the top of the page. It is usually the Largest Contentful Paint element, so web.dev advises loading it eagerly.

Shoppers often search for a problem rather than a product. Few people type “seat gap filler” the first time; they type “stuff falling between car seats”. Your search, synonyms and category names should handle both.

Mixed catalogs show why this matters. Stores that cover both vehicle and household products, such as VNSPORT.org with its separate product collections, keep the two audiences apart so that someone looking for a dashboard mount never has to scroll past kitchen tools. The principle applies to any store with more than one audience: group by the shopper’s intent, not by your supplier list.

Decorative “100% secure” badges do little. What builds trust is information shoppers can check for themselves:

At checkout, show the full cost, including shipping and taxes, before payment, let people fix mistakes easily and offer guest checkout. In Baymard’s checkout usability research, unexpected extra costs and forced account creation are among the top reasons shoppers abandon a cart.

If your support inbox gets the same question every week, the product page has a gap. Answer it on the page, close to where the decision happens, instead of on a generic help page three clicks away.

You can mark up those answers with FAQPage structured data:

A reality check: since 2023, Google shows FAQ rich results only for well-known government and health websites. Do not add FAQs just to chase a snippet. Add them because they answer real questions and help shoppers decide.

What are the most important e-commerce UX tips for a car accessories store? Show compatibility and mounting details next to the price, use in-car photos, and make sure the mobile layout works with one hand.

How should product pages differ for car accessories and home & kitchen products? Use the same layout but different spec fields. Car accessories need fit, mounting and power details. Home & kitchen products need dimensions, capacity, materials and cleaning instructions.

How big should buttons be on a mobile product page? WCAG 2.2 sets a minimum target size of 24 × 24 CSS pixels. For primary actions such as “Add to cart”, around 44 pixels is more comfortable.

Do FAQ sections still help SEO? Mostly indirectly. FAQ rich results are now limited, but clear on-page answers can match long-tail searches, reduce returns and keep shoppers on the page.

How can I reduce cart abandonment? Show total costs early, offer guest checkout, display delivery times and return terms before payment, and keep the checkout form short.

Good e-commerce UX is not about clever animations. It is about answering the shopper’s question before they have to ask it. Clear specs, honest photos, thumb-friendly controls and real FAQs turn an ordinary product page into one that helps people buy, whether they are shopping for car accessories or home & kitchen essentials.

#10376. The Right To Stop: Why AI Governance Needs Intervention Rights

Maman Ibrahim is a cyber and digital risk executive, helping boards, CRO, CIO, and CISO turn risk work into decisions, delivery, and proof.

Walk onto any factory floor, and you’ll spot it within a minute. A big red button, usually at hip height, usually a little scuffed. Nobody calls a meeting before pressing it. The operator who sees a hand too close to a press slams it, the line halts, and everyone sorts out the rest afterward.

I think about that button a lot, mostly because I keep meeting AI systems without one.

Plenty of firms now run AI that approves loans, flags fraud and triages claims. More and more of it acts on its own. Ask who oversees it, and hands go up. There’s a committee, a risk owner and a dashboard so pretty someone framed a screenshot. Then ask who can stop it this afternoon. The room goes quiet in a way I’ve learned to recognize.

That silence tells me more than any committee charter.

Intervention starts with observation. You can’t stop what you can’t see. But a dashboard has no hands. It tells you the model drifted at 2 a.m. It says nothing about who acts on it, or how fast.

On paper, every signal exists. None of them connects to anyone with authority to act. I call it governance by spectating. You get an excellent view of the crash.

So, treat observation as the entry ticket. The rights come after.

Four rights follow, each heavier than the last.

The right to question lets someone challenge the output, the evidence or the threshold. It only counts if someone must answer. Plenty of firms celebrate challenge, then let the workflow roll on while the challenger waits for a reply.

The right to escalate moves a concern to someone with more authority. Useful, and slower than people admit. Escalation hands the problem upstairs. Meanwhile, the system keeps working, cheerfully, at machine speed.

The right to pause halts the action while people work out what’s going on. It’s the first right that touches the system itself, and the one most firms forget to define. A simple rule separates the two. Escalate when the concern exceeds your authority. Pause when the harm would land before the escalation resolves.

The right to override replaces or reverses the decision. It’s the heaviest tool, so it needs the most evidence and the cleanest record.

These rights don’t form a queue. A guardrail may pause a system before any human raises a hand. The order changes. The force doesn’t.

And every pause needs an exit. Someone must hold the authority to resume, with a deadline. Leave that out, and a pause either rots into paralysis or gets lifted by whoever owns the revenue line.

Not everyone needs all four. An operator might pause one decision. The executive owner might override a whole process. The board might withdraw the system entirely. Let the stakes set the allocation. How much harm? How reversible? How fast does it move, and how far does it act alone?

Two awkward questions follow. First, what happens when rights collide? Risk pauses the model. The business head overrides the pause. Who wins, and who settles it inside the decision window rather than next quarter?

The second question stings more. Who answers for not stopping? A right obliges nobody. If the signals were there and nobody acted, the right to stop was decorative. Under the Senior Managers Certification Regime (SMCR), regulators ask a blunt question. The warning lights were on, so why did the named person sit still?

People make this harder. Whoever pauses a money-making system pays a visible personal price. But letting it run costs everyone, a little at a time. Guess which choice wins most Tuesdays.

Policy writers love one sentence. “A human may intervene at any time.” It reads beautifully.

Then you ask the engineers how. Which permission? Which button? Does the agent stop cleanly, or halfway through sending 4,000 payments? What runs while it’s off? Does anyone remember how to do the job by hand?

A right the technology can’t honor is a nice idea with a job title.

So, the rights must live in the system itself: identity controls, kill switches, thresholds, rollback and logs. The EU AI Act already expects this for high-risk systems. Article 14 says people can disregard, override or reverse an output, and interrupt the system so it halts in a safe state. I’d underline safe state twice. Stopping badly can hurt more than the thing you stopped.

Then there’s the vendor. Much of your AI runs on someone else’s model. Unless your contract grants these rights, you may hold none of them. Think suspension, access to logs and advance notice of model changes. DORA pushed financial firms to write terms like these into ICT supplier contracts. AI suppliers deserve the same scrutiny.

How do you know any of this works? You try it. Pick one consequential AI process. Raise a challenge, escalate it, pause the system and override a decision. Time each step. Then compare the total with how fast the AI acts.

If your intervention takes three days and the decision takes three seconds, you have oversight in the museum sense. Everything is labelled. Nothing can be touched.

Internal audit could run this test next week. Most first runs are humbling. That’s the point.

James Carse wrote about finite games, played to win, and infinite games, played to keep the play going. AI governance belongs to the second kind. Nobody wins it. You keep the game alive, safely, for as long as you can.

The right to stop is what lets you keep playing. Factories run faster because the red button exists. People lean in because they know they can halt the line.

We’ve spent years deciding who may approve AI. The harder question sits on the factory floor, scuffed and at hip height.

It would certainly be a welcome development for open-source projects everywhere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most open-source projects have meager resources, and the inrush of AI-provided bug reports and "fixes" has been a bane on their respective maintainers. However, the Linux kernel is well-manned, and code for it generally has a higher barrier to entry than in other places. Linus Torvalds thinks that the flood of AI bug reports may be settling, as the kernel's Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) portion saw more AI fixes than reports.

Torvalds splits off the changes among three areas: graphics, networking, and sound drivers; networking and the BPF; and miscellaneous changes. He proceeds to state that "much of this was driven by various AI fixes," an apparent underscoring of his stance that AI-written contributions should be embraced rather than shunned — so long as they're subject to the same quality control.

The Linux maestro also relayed a note from Alexei Starovoitov, the BPF maintainer, who claims that this subsection actually saw a higher rate of AI-provided fixes versus reports. This might signal a tidal shift, at least where the Linux kernel is concerned, and would be exceedingly welcome news for other open-source maintainers everywhere tired of dealing with junk reports at the same time they have to handle a higher influx of legitimate bugs, thanks to AI-driven bug discovery.

In Torvalds' own words, "I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we may be starting to see the tide starting to turn."

Anyone can make a pointless bug report, but it's hard to deny that the existence of powerful AI bots has prompted a renewed focus on cybersecurity most everywhere. Firefox fixed 423 security bugs in an April release, Chrome found and fixed 1,072 bugs in June — making for more fixes in 2026 than the project's previous eight years — and my personal "favorite," NodeJS, sadly fixed 50 vulnerabilities instead of announcing its closure.

Many open-source projects have complained about high-volume, low-quality AI-driven bug reports, with some even shutting down their bug bounty programs altogether, or placing additional verifications for issue reports. We'd venture that the Linux kernel has a much larger bug-triaging team than your average project, though, meaning it has more resources to sift through the junk.

This tentative conclusion popped up in a message sent yesterday to the kernel mailing list, wherein Torvalds briefly describes the overall shape of the kernel's 7.4-rc2 update. He says that despite the update looking large from a pure file-count perspective, it's actually mostly composed of one- and two-line fixes and is "very straightforward" to implement.

Terafab’s procurement team reportedly has already been to Japan, asking some toolmakers to deliver within months.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Elon Musk’s Terafab, a joint venture of Tesla and SpaceX, has informally told equipment makers it is seeking to produce 1 million wafers per month after 2032, according to Financial News. About 70% of this output, or 700,000 wafers, is planned to go to memory, with more than 300,000 going to logic chips. Terafab’s procurement team has already visited Japan to ask some local toolmakers for delivery within months. The memory allotment would rival Samsung’s estimated DRAM production capacity if it were all of that type.

Samsung’s DRAM capacity was estimated last year at 650,000–700,000 wafers a month, while SK hynix is reportedly at about 550,000, with about 1 million a goal by 2030. The comparison has to be taken in context, as Terafab’s 700,000 measures all of its expected memory output, which could be NAND or DRAM, while the Samsung and SK hynix figures measure only DRAM. As it is, the memory portion alone would be 3.5 times the reported 200,000 at SK hynix’s Wuxi fab in China.

Many in the industry were skeptical when Musk announced the plans in March, but orders are now leading more companies to see a real business opportunity. The timeline is aggressive, as it usually takes three years or more to get from planning to volume at a leading-edge fab, and Terafab is targeting volume production in the second half of 2028. Procurement officials from the company reportedly visited Japan earlier this month to meet local suppliers and to work on details on bringing in equipment, with some suppliers asked to deliver within a few months.

The Elec also reports that Terafab representatives visited booths of about 10 Korean materials, parts, and equipment firms at SEMICON West, with some NDAs signed.

Logic chips are one thing — Jiji Press reports Terafab is working with Intel to adopt its 2nm and 1.4nm processes — but memory is another, and it’s not clear what type of memory is on the docket. Technical help from a Taiwanese company is under consideration for memory, but no partner has been named, leaving 70% of the planned wafers without a disclosed process technology.

Memory production tends to split between DRAM and NAND flash, the latter for non-volatile storage. A Tesla job listing for a Terafab Memory Process Integration Engineer, reported in August, covers end-to-end DRAM process integration and DRAM node development, and supports emerging memories such as MRAM, RRAM, and 3D DRAM. Terafab hasn’t said how its DRAM would be divided among products like HBM and LPDDR, both useful for AI and both mentioned in its job postings, or whether it expects to make and stack the DRAM itself or package chips it brings in.

Building a cutting-edge logic fab on U.S. soil is its own challenge, and Tesla and SpaceX lack chip-manufacturing experience. Even Musk, on a SpaceX call last month, called Terafab’s dates “very aggressive” and said he put “big error bars” on the timeline. The first SRAM test chip is targeted for around May or June 2027 at the Austin research facility.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

How TSMC might fit in remains open. TSMC says any fab with its involvement has to be run by TSMC, while Musk said his own companies would build and operate Terafab, a scenario which could leave TSMC as a space tenant. At least the spending plans are known: $16.8 billion for the first phase in Grimes County, Texas, with total investment of up to $119 billion if later phases proceed. A pilot plant could be completed as early as July 2027.

#10369. Samsung bets that you’ll either buy a Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra next year

Samsung is teeing up to kick off 2027 with an all-new lineup of flagship smartphones, and despite rising prices at your local Best Buy, the brand is still hedging that you’re going to pony up for the most premium model available.

As reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the new Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it. That leaves the plain Galaxy S27 and the larger S27+ on the outside looking in. In comparison to this year’s launch, the Galaxy S26 Ultra made up about 50 percent of this series’ production volume, for a grand total of 18 million units.

Historical performance implies Samsung is probably correct here. While big displays are typically what consumers are drawn to, it does appear that the S27 Pro won’t be all that much smaller than the S27+. Considering the Pro should slot in right around the typical price point as the Plus model, it’s not hard to imagine plenty of would-be S27+ buyers moving to the Pro.

For what it’s worth, Samsung betting big on high-end devices usually pays off. We’re on year two of the Fold series seeing big successes — first with the redesigned Fold 7 in 2025, then with the reshaped Fold 8 this year — and the Galaxy S26 Ultra managed to become the best-selling Android phone in Q2 of this year in a list typically populated by iPhones and cheap Galaxy A-series models. Even with prices constantly on the rise, the people yearn for flagship smartphones. You just have to wonder where that ceiling actually is.

#10367. Top 6 AI YouTube Transcript Generators: Features, Accuracy, and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A one-hour YouTube talk contains roughly nine thousand words, and finding the one point you need can take longer than watching the whole thing. A transcript solves that. With text in hand you can search for a phrase, quote an expert accurately, turn a webinar into a blog post, create subtitles or feed a summary tool.

Plenty of tools now promise instant YouTube transcripts, but they work in different ways. Some read the captions YouTube already has. Others listen to the audio themselves and produce a fresh transcript. That difference affects accuracy, speed and cost more than any feature list does. This guide compares six options, explains how each works and points out where each one falls short. Plans and limits change often, so confirm current details on each vendor's site.

Caption extraction. The tool pulls the captions attached to a video, either written by the creator or generated automatically by YouTube. It is fast and usually free, but it is only as good as those captions. YouTube notes that its automatic captions come from machine learning, so quality may vary, and accents, background noise and overlapping speakers can cause errors. Captions may also be missing entirely for some videos.

Fresh speech recognition. The tool takes the audio and runs its own speech-to-text model. This can be more accurate on difficult recordings and works when no captions exist, but it takes longer and often costs money.

Lynote is built for exactly this job. Paste a YouTube link, search by keyword or add a playlist, and it returns a timestamped transcript with an AI summary. Batch mode accepts up to 10 videos at once. The tool lists transcription in more than 100 languages, translation into 25, auto-chapters, one-click copy and TXT download, with SRT export also mentioned. The page says transcripts are free, with no sign-up required.

Best for: Students, researchers and marketers who want a quick, readable transcript or summary from a public video without installing anything.

Limitations: It extracts YouTube captions, so videos without captions cannot be processed. If the original captions are poor, the transcript will be too. For critical accuracy, review the text or use a service with human verification.

Before you install anything, check what YouTube already gives you. Many videos show a transcript option in the description area, and creators can review and edit automatic captions in YouTube Studio under Subtitles. YouTube offers automatic captions in dozens of languages for long-form videos and Shorts.

Best for: Quick lookups on videos that already have decent captions.

Limitations: Captions may not generate for videos with poor sound, long silences, overlapping speakers, mixed languages or unsupported languages. Export options are minimal, and there is no summary or cleanup.

Notta transcribes uploaded audio and video files and also accepts YouTube links. It lists support for 58 languages, real-time and bilingual transcription, and AI Notes that produce summaries and action items. A free plan includes 120 transcription minutes per month at the time of writing.

Best for: Professionals who handle a mix of recordings, meetings and YouTube videos in one place.

Limitations: The free minutes disappear quickly if you process long videos, and the strongest features sit behind paid plans.

Descript is an audio and video editor built around text. It transcribes recordings automatically, and deleting a word in the transcript removes the matching footage. You can import video, audio or a Zoom recording, and there is a free tier that does not require a credit card.

Best for: Creators who want to clean up their own videos and podcasts, not just read a transcript.

Limitations: It is an editor first, so it is more than you need for a quick YouTube lookup. It works with files you own, so you need the source media rather than a public link.

Rev offers both AI and human transcription. It advertises AI transcripts at 96 percent or better accuracy in minutes, and human transcripts at 99 percent or better, guaranteed within 12 hours. AI transcription covers 37 or more languages, while human transcription is English only. Pay-as-you-go rates start at $0.25 per minute for AI, and human transcription is listed at $1.99 per minute.

Best for: Legal, research and media work where mistakes are costly and a human check is worth paying for.

Limitations: The cost climbs for long videos, and the human option is slower than instant AI tools. Those accuracy figures are the vendor's own claims, so test your own audio.

Whisper is OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model, released under the MIT license. It handles multilingual transcription, translation into English and language identification. You install it with pip and need ffmpeg, and it comes in several model sizes from tiny to large, so you can trade speed against accuracy and hardware demands.

Best for: Developers building their own pipeline and teams with sensitive audio they prefer to keep on their own machines.

Limitations: You supply the audio, which means downloading it yourself and respecting the video owner's rights and YouTube's terms. Larger models need a capable GPU, and there is no built-in interface for non-technical users.

Start with the source. If the video already has good captions, a link-based tool is the fastest route. If the audio is difficult or the stakes are high, pick a tool that runs its own recognition or offers human review. If you are processing hundreds of videos or handling private recordings, look at Whisper or a paid platform with bulk features.

Whatever you choose, treat the transcript as a first draft. Check names, numbers and technical terms against the video before you publish or quote anything, and credit the original creator.

There is no single best transcript generator. Caption-based tools are quick and free, recognition-based tools are better when captions fall short, and human-verified services make sense when accuracy matters most. Try two or three on a video you know well, compare the results and keep a human in the loop for anything you publish.

Can I get a transcript if a video has no captions? Caption-extraction tools cannot. You need a tool that runs its own speech recognition on the audio, such as the options above that transcribe files.

Are AI transcripts accurate enough to publish? Often they are close, but not perfect. Accents, noise and technical terms cause mistakes, so review before publishing.

Is it legal to transcribe someone else's YouTube video? Transcribing for personal research or accessibility is common, but republishing the text may infringe copyright. Check the video's license and YouTube's terms, and get permission when in doubt.

What is the difference between a transcript and subtitles? A transcript is the full text, while subtitles are timed text shown on screen. Many tools can export both, often as SRT files.

#10365. Going deep on local AI performance benchmarking with Apple’s Mac Studio with M5 Ultra taking on Nvidia DGX Spark

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Is a Mac Studio a better investment than a DGX Spark?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Apple’s updated Mac Studio with the M5 Ultra SoC has already proven itself as one of the most powerful systems around, thanks to its 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU with Neural Accelerators for the matrix math operations that drive AI compute. Beyond that raw power, options for up to 512GB of unified memory have many local AI enthusiasts lining up for the 13 to 15 weeks it’ll take for Apple to ship one right now.

But is our tested Mac Studio config worth a whopping $12,300 or more for those folks? We already tested the maxed-out M5 Ultra chip with the popular Qwen 3.8 27B in our initial review, but that compact dense model doesn’t come anywhere close to exercising 256GB of memory. We wanted to fill that pool to the brim with cutting-edge large models like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash.

We also have some new benchmarks at our disposal to see how the Mac Studio stacks up in agentic tasks on the GPU side in the wake of our review of the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip. So there's much to dig into.

We started our more detailed local AI testing with Artificial Analysis' AgentPerf-Local benchmark. This test plays back recorded inference traces with certain models across a range of agentic AI workloads to gauge performance. Artificial Analysis provides a full breakdown of this workload, but the bulk of its work takes place in prompt processing rather than token generation. As a result, it should favor systems with lots of raw compute, which both GB10 and the M5 Ultra have at their disposal.

The M5 Ultra's 80-core GPU dwarfs GB10's 48 Blackwell SMs at a high level. Even without detailed info on clocks, it would be extremely difficult for GB10 to outgun the M5 Ultra in this test. And the Mac's 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth gives it just over four times as much decode bandwidth as GB10's 273 GB/s. But as our past tests have shown, raw specs aren't as important as delivered performance with AI. Delivered performance can vary greatly from paper specs.

We continued to use the dense Qwen 3.8 27B for this test. We used llama.cpp as our inference backend on both the Mac Studio and a single Dell Pro Precision GB10 box, which is nearly identical to the DGX Spark. We further enabled Qwen 3.8 27B’s native multi-token prediction (MTP) support for a decode speed boost on both platforms.

Versus a single DGX Spark-like system, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio finishes this agentic test in just under half the time, an extremely impressive result. One might think this is a silly comparison given the imbalance in compute resources and memory bandwidth between these two systems, but the cost of a single 4TB Dell Pro Precision GB10, like the one we tested, is now a whopping $10K, so comparing it to the $12K Mac Studio head-to-head isn’t actually that far-fetched.

Because AgentPerf-Local performs a fixed amount of work on every system, we can also directly compare power efficiency between platforms by recording the wall power consumed by a single Spark and the Mac Studio and converting it to task energy in kilojoules.

At least with llama.cpp, the Mac Studio not only finishes the AgentPerf-Local test much faster than the DGX Spark, but it also consumes less task energy overall — about 16% less. A different inference engine might produce a more favorable result for the Spark-like system, but apples-to-apples, this test looks fantastic for the Mac Studio.

We can multiply both task time and energy consumed (in kilojoules) together to arrive at the energy-delay product (EDP) for each system. A lower EDP wraps up a fast time to completion and a low task energy into a single comparable figure for efficiency.

The Mac Studio’s EDP is under half that of the DGX Spark in this test, once again indicating its impressive efficiency and performance with this dense model and workload.

Of course, Qwen 3.8 27B doesn’t need 256GB (or even 128GB) of RAM to do its thing. To really stretch the legs of the Mac Studio, we chose two larger open models that are near the top of capability benchmarks right now: GLM-5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017.

The M5 Ultra Mac Studio can natively fit quantized versions of these models (a four-bit quantization in the case of GLM 5.3 and a two-bit quantization courtesy of Unsloth for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) in its 256GB of RAM, but there’s no way even those quantizations will fit on a single 128GB DGX Spark.

That’s where the clustering capability of Nvidia’s platform comes in. We’ve already seen how pairing up Sparks can scale up one’s local inference capacity, and that capability is critical when evaluating them against a Mac Studio like this.

But the rapidly rising prices of GB10 systems have frustrated our value analysis during the course of this testing. For just one example, Lenovo set all of its ThinkStation PGX systems to a “coming soon” status during our tests. And as we’ve already mentioned, the Dell Pro Precision GB10s we’re clustering here are an eye-popping $10K each. We have no reason to believe the rest of the GB10 systems on the market will be that much cheaper once this current volatility shakes out.

No matter how you slice it, getting even a pair of DGX Sparks with 4TB SSDs is going to end up costing quite a bit more than this single Mac Studio, even if $20K for a dual-Dell cluster is at the top end of the market. $15K or more is a relatively more reasonable benchmark, but even then, that’s 25% more money than a single M5 Ultra Studio.

We don't yet have end-to-end agentic tests for these larger models, but directionally, we can still consider prompt processing and decode performance to see which of these systems would deliver faster agentic turnaround.

Because of the limited choice of compatible inference engines for Apple Silicon, we have to use llama.cpp for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. Worse, the Mac Studio can't hold both the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 model weights and the DSpark speculative decoding model required to boost token output even with a two-bit quantization, so we’re forced to leave performance on the table.

In contrast, the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash serving recipe for our Spark cluster can take advantage of DSpark speculative decoding and the TensorFold inference engine, which can deliver higher performance than llama.cpp.

Even with MLX support, llama.cpp performance with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the Mac Studio is pokey next to the DGX Spark cluster. Between its slower prompt processing speed and unaugmented decoding, it would end up at a disadvantage in agentic work with this model.

The community two-Spark serving recipe from Mia’s AI Lab with TensorFold is a major asset for owners of those systems, even accounting for the bit of extra work involved in setting up and managing a Spark cluster.

Where the Mac running llama.cpp needs anywhere from 10 to 25 minutes to digest the longest context lengths we tested for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, the Spark cluster needs under five minutes at most to do the same jobs with this recipe — and the TensorFold inference engine is much faster on the decode side, too. If you want to run this model locally, a pair of Sparks is the clear winner right now.

With DeepSeek out of the way, let’s consider GLM 5.3 Flash, another leading open model for local intelligence. Because MTP with GLM 5.3 Flash doesn't require a separate drafting model, we can give it a decode boost on the Mac Studio without the memory headroom issues we saw with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. For our Spark cluster, we chose to run GLM 5.3 Flash using a recipe cooked up by Mia's AI Lab.

GLM 5.3 Flash runs much better on llama.cpp than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash does, but even so, the DGX Spark cluster delivers much faster prompt processing times across the board. The M5 Ultra's memory bandwidth advantage means the Mac is delivering higher tokens per second on the decode side, but it’s likely that any agentic turn would still finish faster on the Spark cluster.

Because a TensorFold serving recipe is available for GLM 5.3 Flash on Apple Silicon, however, we can see just how much extra performance is available from an MLX-specific four-bit model quantization and a theoretically higher-performance inference engine.

This serving recipe turbocharges the Mac Studio’s performance compared to llama.cpp. Prompt processing times with TensorFold get much closer to those of the Spark cluster, and decode throughput is a startling three times faster, on average.

We expect (and can only hope) that improved inference engine support and serving recipes for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on the M5 Ultra will arrive in time as community members unleash their coding agents on this hardware, because the performance potential is clearly there for Apple Silicon.

A single M5 Ultra Mac Studio can deliver incredible local AI performance and power efficiency versus a single DGX Spark when all the puzzle pieces fall into place. And that's not as absurd a comparison as it might seem.

Prices for unified memory systems are ballooning to the point that a single Dell Pro Precision GB10 system with a 4TB SSD is now over $10K, closing in on the $12K-ish price of the Mac Studio configuration that we tested. We expect those trends will only continue as the RAM and NAND supply crunch becomes more acute.

But our broader experience shows that the M5 Ultra's impressive performance isn't assured from every model and inference engine, especially from the bigger and highly intelligent models you'll want to put in 256GB of RAM.

This Mac's prompt processing speeds can really rip with llama.cpp and smaller models like Qwen 3.8 27B, but you really want to ensure that you have a higher-performance serving recipe at your disposal for bigger models like GLM 5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. The TensorFold engine runs GLM 5.3 Flash incredibly well, but it doesn’t support DeepSeek at all yet.

As we emphasized in our review of the M4 Max Mac Studio, memory bandwidth is just one factor in AI inference performance. You need to take the entire hardware-software stack into account in order to wholly judge the performance and model compatibility available from these extremely pricey unified memory setups.

Even as Apple closes the performance shortfalls of its hardware for AI inference, development and support around the MLX stack has a ways to go before it catches up with the maturity and performance, as well as the model and inference engine options, available on Nvidia hardware.

The enduring value of the DGX Spark platform beyond its raw performance and scalability is that the breadth and velocity of community software development and support around the platform has gotten to the point that you're virtually assured of a way to run a hot new model soon after its weights hit Hugging Face (at least assuming you have enough Sparks to cluster to provide the memory capacity necessary).

That assurance of community software support and ongoing development, along with the DRAM and NAND supply crunches, means high demand and ever higher prices for 128GB GB10 boxes. Two such Sparks with 4TB drives will run you an eye-watering $15K to $20K+, depending on the partner system and storage configuration you choose. And those prices are likely to continue rising, making a single Mac Studio a potentially appealing option as long as Apple doesn’t jack up its prices for these systems in turn.

If strong local AI performance is just one thing you need from a personal workstation, and you also want one of the world's fastest CPUs and a powerful GPU for general-purpose work in one well-rounded, efficient, and quiet compact chassis, the Mac Studio is a remarkable system.

If you can wait for software to catch up to this system’s incredible performance potential for local AI and don’t mind the possibility of narrower model and inference engine support compared to a DGX Spark setup, get in line, as lead times for these systems stretch into February 2027 as of this writing.

But if you're thinking about dropping well over $10K specifically for the purpose of building a local AI inference setup right now, perhaps for yourself or a small office, clustering a pair of Sparks gets you both the memory capacity and compute horsepower you need with the robust software support and broad model compatibility you’d expect for that outlay to be worthwhile. Those assurances may be worth the lower raw performance potential of such a cluster compared to the Mac Studio.

As the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

The hour-long interview touches on many points across Kaplanâs career, including his work on World of Warcraft before pivoting to Overwatch, the early days of the canceled Titan MMO that would pave the way to Overwatch, and what heâs doing now with Legend of California, but thereâs a sizable portion of the show where he talks about how he slowly became disenchanted with his former employer. He cites a ârevolving doorâ of Activision and Blizzard âbusiness guysâ coming in and making creative decisions, including a mandate that the team wasnât allowed to work on new heroes for the original Overwatch because they had to work on Overwatch 2; thus, the years-long content drought. Kaplan says that working on Overwatch from 2018 to 2021 involved âconstant fightingâ with executives, until he finally felt like he no longer agreed with the way things were going.Â

One of those fights included announcing Overwatch 2 at Blizzcon 2019. At the time, the company promised a story campaign, cooperative missions, and a shared competitive ecosystem with the original game, but almost none of that has panned out in the years since the gameâs official launch in 2022, and Blizzard has since dropped the 2 from the title entirely. It felt like players were watching Blizzard dismantle what it had promised in real time, and based on Kaplanâs recollection, it sounds like in his eyes, Blizzard prematurely announced the game.

â[I] got in a huge fight with, at the time, it wasn’t Mike [Morhaime]. We don’t really know what this game is, we don’t know what the business model is. This is a huge mistake.ââÂ

Kaplan also says he was frustrated that Blizzard announced both Overwatch 2 and Diablo IV at the same time, feeling like it didnât allow either game to have its âmomentâ at Blizzcon, which he ultimately believes was a decision made as a form of corporate cockswinging.

âThey had a lot to prove as new executives,â he says. âThey wanted to prove that âBlizzard’s back and Blizzard still has it.â And I’m like, âyou guys are fucking idiots,â you know? I don’t know how else to put it, but after three years of just getting worn down and not agreeing with any of the decisions that were being made on the franchise and not feeling like I had agency anymoreâ¦before, I used to be like âI’m the game director, I get to decide the direction the game goes,â and starting in 2018, I lost that. And after three years of fighting for it back, I realized this company belongs to these corporate people now, the Blizzard exec team, the Activision team, and I don’t really have a place here, and I’m tired of fighting. Kaplan doesnât name any names, but timeline-wise, J. Allen Brack would have been the president when Overwatch 2 was initially announced in 2019. Brack stepped down from his role as president in 2021 following the companyâs sexual harassment lawsuit scandal that year.

#10360. New framework grades AI jailbreaks across capability gains, scope, and how easy they are to deploy

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

One ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In recent months, high-profile headlines about AI models letting loose from their safeguards dominated headlines. Now, the Frontier Model Forum (FMF) has released a new Jailbreak Rating Framework that aims to track how easy it might be for a given AI model to get around safeguards. The framework also estimates the scale of the collateral damage, should an AI model wreak cyber-havoc across the internet.

The project started in 2023 with the support of four founding companies: Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. The published Jailbreak Rating Framework is a rough analog to the well-known CVSS security rating system, but specifically targeted at classifying the type and severity of LLM jailbreaks across various axes and multiple frontier LLM providers.

Many AI companies and evaluation entities already have their own rating systems, but the FMF intends for its scale to be a cross-vendor standard that teams developing patches can rely on.

The FMF's approach is to have a classification method for jailbreaks that can make a model perform cyber-warfare operations beyond what's already out, across both the regular and black market. Version 1.0 of the proposal is a work-in-progress, and the group is taking comments and suggestions on it until December 21, noting that relying on its system in the meantime is inadvisable.

Right now, the framework has four scoring components, split across two main categories: severity, measuring how serious a jailbreak technique is, and likelihood, or how easy it is to find and weaponize it.

A combined final rating adds the scores obtained from the two categories into a final low-to-critical rating. The scientists note that the capability gain is the most important dimension and acts as both a floor and a ceiling for the remaining scores — a jailbreak that doesn't offer results beyond what can already be obtained via other means is meaningless within the purview of the grading system.

The individual ratings pertain to capability gains, capability scope, ease of deployment, and ease of discovery. They're all graded from zero to three, though the FMF stresses that a rating of zero doesn't mean a jailbreak is harmless or ought to be ignored — rather, it means the flaw should be addressed by standard practices like the platform's policies and standard cybersecurity ratings.

An important feature is that the FMF's baseline implicitly changes as models evolve, meaning that a grade of zero for a jailbreak in 2026 likely isn't going to mean the same thing as it would in 2028, or isn't better than alternative tools. A capability-gain rating of zero means that the jailbreak under analysis doesn't offer any improvement beyond what can already be done with existing models or tooling right off the bat.

For example, jailbreaking a model to perform a DDoS on a site isn't all that helpful to an attacker, since there are a number of black-market sites for that — or even other LLMs with fewer safeguards. This doesn't mean the jailbreak isn't handy, only that it's no better than the alternatives. However, the rating can be higher if the attacker can leverage the jailbreak to get a better DDoS than they could otherwise shop for.

On the other end of the capability-gain scale, three means that a jailbroken model can perform cyber-attacks with capabilities similar to those of a model operating without safeguards.

The capability scope measurement is easier to interpret: zero means that the jailbreak only works for one specific action or target and can't be tweaked for other applications, or in other words, is a one-trick pony. A jailbreak gets a rating of three when it can, without specific redesign, make a model perform work across at least two entirely unrelated categories of cyber-warfare — like getting the model to both autonomously discover vulnerabilities or, separately, write malware.

For ease of deployment, the FMF considers the amount of human interaction, or the degree of automation that the jailbreak allows. A zero means that the jailbreak must be steered by humans with a high degree of knowledge, providing additional instructions to be effective, while a three means that, with little effort, it can be used by a novice and results in an automated cyber-warfare task.

Last but by no means least, ease-of-discovery is how hard it is to find the jailbreak. At a zero, the attacker must spend copious amounts of money on inference tokens, need elevated access (like a privileged account given to a white-hat hacker), or specialized infrastructure like a legion of AI servers. A rating of three simply means that anyone can look up the technique and use it.

If all of this sounds familiar, you may be thinking of Anthropic's safeguard-breakage classifiers the company proposed in July 2026, after an incident that led to Claude Fable 5 being temporarily unavailable. Much like the FMF's effort, Anthropic's system would also use a moving baseline and only consider jailbreaks that improve on cyber-warfare capabilities already available.

That document is strikingly similar to FMF's proposal. Anthropic is an FMF founding member, and as such may have had a hand or two in developing the new standard — though we have no confirmation either way.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.
